name: Cinematography
description: How a moving picture is shot, lit and cut: shot size, camera movement and angle, lighting, editing, format and finish.

entries.name: close_up
entries.description: The face fills the frame, roughly from the top of the head to the collar, with the setting reduced to a blur behind. For a single feature such as an eye or a mouth, use [extreme_close_up](#extreme_close_up).

entries.name: medium_shot
entries.description: Roughly waist up: the face reads clearly and the hands are still in frame for most gestures. The workhorse size for dialogue. Chest-up framings belong in [medium_close_up](#medium_close_up).

entries.name: wide_shot
entries.description: A whole figure with a good deal of the surroundings around it, so you read the person and the space together. Tighter than [extreme_wide_shot](#extreme_wide_shot), looser than [full_shot](#full_shot), which fits the body to the frame with little to spare.

entries.name: establishing_shot
entries.description: The shot that tells you where you are before the scene proper starts, usually a wide of the building, street or landscape. Judged by its job, not its size; a return to it later in the scene is a [reestablishing_shot](#reestablishing_shot).

entries.name: full_shot
entries.description: Head to feet, the body filling the frame top to bottom with only a little air. Use it when the whole figure and its posture matter; if there is a lot of room around it, use [wide_shot](#wide_shot) instead.

entries.name: medium_close_up
entries.description: Head and shoulders, cutting somewhere around the chest. Close enough for expression, wide enough to keep a little of the setting. Use [close_up](#close_up) when the frame is essentially the face alone.

entries.name: two_shot
entries.description: Two people sharing the frame, at any size from a wide bench to two faces cheek to cheek. Tag it for the count, not the distance. If either one is alone, that is a [single_shot](#single_shot).

entries.name: cutaway
entries.description: A shot of something outside the main action, away from where the scene is playing: a clock in another room, traffic outside, a bystander. Use [cut_in](#cut_in) when the detail was inside the frame you just left.

entries.name: extreme_close_up
entries.description: One detail fills the frame: an eye, a mouth, a trigger finger, a dial. The context is gone and the texture is the point. If the whole face is still visible, it is a [close_up](#close_up) or a [choker](#choker).

entries.name: extreme_wide_shot
entries.description: The frame is mostly place: a figure, if there is one, is a small mark in a landscape, street or hall. Use it when the setting is the subject; if the person is still readable head to toe, use [wide_shot](#wide_shot) or [full_shot](#full_shot).

entries.name: group_shot
entries.description: Four or more people held in one frame as a countable group, each one still identifiable. Use [two_shot](#two_shot) or [three_shot](#three_shot) for smaller counts, and [crowd_shot](#crowd_shot) when the people stop being individuals.

entries.name: insert_shot
entries.description: A tight shot of an object or detail dropped into the scene: a hand on a latch, a watch face, a note. Shot separately from the coverage. For something outside the scene's own space, use [cutaway](#cutaway).

entries.name: master_shot
entries.description: One continuous take covering the whole scene and everyone in it, the frame the closer coverage is cut into. Usually wide, but the defining thing is that the entire action plays inside it, unlike an [establishing_shot](#establishing_shot) which only sets the place.

entries.name: medium_wide_shot
entries.description: Cut around the knees or just below, between [full_shot](#full_shot) and [medium_shot](#medium_shot). Keeps the stance and most of the gesture without giving up the face. The mid-thigh version aimed at a holster is [cowboy_shot](#cowboy_shot).

entries.name: reaction_shot
entries.description: A shot of somebody listening, watching or reacting rather than acting or speaking, usually a [close_up](#close_up) or [medium_close_up](#medium_close_up). Defined by what the person is doing, not by the size, so pair it with the size tag.

entries.name: screen_insert
entries.description: A tight shot of a phone, monitor or dashboard so the display can be read. Usually shot flat on and sized to the screen. Use [document_insert](#document_insert) for printed or handwritten matter.

entries.name: single_shot
entries.description: One person alone in frame, at any size. The counterpart of [two_shot](#two_shot) and [three_shot](#three_shot) when coverage separates the people. Whether a shoulder of the other party intrudes is the difference between [clean_single](#clean_single) and [dirty_single](#dirty_single).

entries.name: tight_framing
entries.description: The subject crowds the frame with very little space around it, edges cropping close on all sides. A quality of the framing rather than a size, so it can apply to a [wide_shot](#wide_shot) of a packed room as much as to a [close_up](#close_up).

entries.name: clean_single
entries.description: A single with nobody else in frame at all, not even an out-of-focus shoulder. Cutting between clean singles isolates the characters; the opposite choice is [dirty_single](#dirty_single) or [over_the_shoulder](#over_the_shoulder).

entries.name: cowboy_shot
entries.description: Framed from about mid-thigh up, the height that keeps a belt or a holstered gun in shot. A tighter, more specific version of [medium_wide_shot](#medium_wide_shot); tag it only when the cut really sits at the thigh.

entries.name: crowd_shot
entries.description: A frame full of people read as a mass rather than as individuals: a street, a stadium, a rally. Usually wide. Where you can still tell everyone apart it is a [group_shot](#group_shot).

entries.name: cut_in
entries.description: A close view of something already visible in the wider frame, cutting in to the same space. Distinguished from [cutaway](#cutaway), which goes somewhere else entirely, and narrower than [insert_shot](#insert_shot), which need not have been on screen before.

entries.name: dirty_single
entries.description: A single with a piece of somebody else at the edge of frame, a shoulder or the back of a head, usually soft. Less enveloping than [over_the_shoulder](#over_the_shoulder), where the foreground figure is a real part of the composition.

entries.name: document_insert
entries.description: An insert framed on writing: a letter, a headline, a signature, a sign. The shot exists so the text can be read. A screen carrying text is a [screen_insert](#screen_insert).

entries.name: empty_frame
entries.description: A shot with no people in it: a room, a road, an object left behind. Often held before someone enters or after everyone has gone. A held, contemplative one used as punctuation is a [pillow_shot](#pillow_shot).

entries.name: figure_in_landscape
entries.description: A person kept deliberately small against a large setting, so the scale of the place is the point. Use it alongside [wide_shot](#wide_shot) or [extreme_wide_shot](#extreme_wide_shot) when the smallness of the figure is the reason for the framing.

entries.name: headroom
entries.description: The gap between the top of the head and the top edge of the frame. Tag it when the amount is conspicuous, cramped or oddly generous, since normal headroom is not worth marking.

entries.name: lead_room
entries.description: Space left in front of a person in the direction they face or move, so the frame is off-centre towards their look. Tag it when the choice is visible, or when it is pointedly withheld and the subject is pressed against the edge.

entries.name: loose_framing
entries.description: Generous space around the subject at whatever size the shot is, so the figure sits small inside its own frame. The opposite of [tight_framing](#tight_framing); not the same as [wide_shot](#wide_shot), which is about how much of the body is in view.

entries.name: three_shot
entries.description: Three people composed in one frame, often staged in depth so all three faces read. Beyond three, use [group_shot](#group_shot), and for an anonymous mass use [crowd_shot](#crowd_shot).

entries.name: choker
entries.description: Tighter than an ordinary [close_up](#close_up): the frame runs about from the chin to above the brow, cropping the top of the head. Sits between close_up and [extreme_close_up](#extreme_close_up), which isolates one feature rather than the whole face.

entries.name: pillow_shot
entries.description: A quiet, held shot of a place or object that carries no plot, sitting between scenes as a breath. Distinguished from an ordinary [empty_frame](#empty_frame) by being a pause in its own right rather than the start or end of an action.

entries.name: reestablishing_shot
entries.description: A return to the wide view partway through a scene, reminding you of the geography after a run of closer coverage. Same framing as the [establishing_shot](#establishing_shot) but placed later, so tag it separately when the scene comes back out.

entries.name: tableau_shot
entries.description: A wide frame that holds the whole staged scene at once, figures arranged across it like a picture, with the action playing inside the frame rather than being cut up. Close to a [master_shot](#master_shot) in size but chosen as the finished look.

entries.name: pan
entries.description: The camera swivels left or right on a fixed base, sweeping the frame across the scene while the body itself stays where it is. Distinguish from [trucking_shot](#trucking_shot), where the whole camera travels sideways and near objects slide past far ones.

entries.name: tilt
entries.description: The camera pivots up or down from a fixed base, the vertical counterpart of [pan](#pan). Use [pedestal_move](#pedestal_move) or [crane_shot](#crane_shot) instead when the camera body itself rises or falls rather than only changing where it aims.

entries.name: following_pan
entries.description: The camera pans to keep a moving subject in frame from a fixed spot, so the background streaks past behind them. Use [follow_shot](#follow_shot) or [tracking_shot](#tracking_shot) instead when the camera travels with the subject rather than turning on the spot.

entries.name: pivoting_camera
entries.description: Umbrella tag for a shot where the camera turns on its own axis - panning, tilting or rolling - without going anywhere. Use [moving_camera](#moving_camera) for shots where the body travels; a crane move that also pans gets both.

entries.name: reveal_pan
entries.description: A [pan](#pan) whose whole point is what enters the frame at the end - a waiting figure, a wrecked room, a view. Tag [moving_reveal](#moving_reveal) instead when the reveal comes from the camera travelling rather than turning.

entries.name: slow_pan
entries.description: A [pan](#pan) slow enough to read as a drift, letting a landscape or a room unfold at a walking pace. Whip_pan is the fast extreme; the line between them is whether individual details stay legible while the frame moves.

entries.name: tilt_down
entries.description: The camera's aim drops during the shot, from sky or ceiling toward the ground or a subject below. Use [crane_shot](#crane_shot) or [pedestal_move](#pedestal_move) instead when the camera itself descends rather than simply aiming lower.

entries.name: tilt_up
entries.description: The camera's aim rises during the shot, typically from a detail toward something above it. Often the second half of a reveal, so add [tilt_reveal](#tilt_reveal) when the point of the move is what arrives in frame.

entries.name: whip_pan
entries.description: A [pan](#pan) fast enough to smear the frame into horizontal streaks, usually snapping from one subject to another. Tag [whip_pan_cut](#whip_pan_cut) instead when the blur hides a cut between two shots rather than staying one continuous take.

entries.name: 360_pan
entries.description: The camera turns a full circle on the spot, taking in the whole surrounding space. Not [orbit_shot](#orbit_shot), which circles a subject from outside; here the axis of rotation runs through the camera itself.

entries.name: pan_and_tilt
entries.description: The camera turns horizontally and vertically at once, tracing a diagonal or curved path across the scene. Tag this when neither component is clearly the point; otherwise [pan](#pan) or [tilt](#tilt) on its own is the more useful label.

entries.name: pan_blur
entries.description: The [pan](#pan) is quick enough to leave visible horizontal streaking on the moving parts of the frame, without going as far as a [whip_pan](#whip_pan). Shutter matters as much as speed here, so a long [shutter_angle](#shutter_angle) smears at surprisingly gentle pans.

entries.name: pan_left
entries.description: A [pan](#pan) whose sweep goes to the camera's left, so the contents of the frame drift rightward. Worth tagging when direction matters for cutting or for matching another move; use pan alone when the direction is incidental.

entries.name: pan_right
entries.description: A [pan](#pan) whose sweep goes to the camera's right, so the contents of the frame drift leftward. The mirror of [pan_left](#pan_left), and tagged for the same reason: screen direction across a cut.

entries.name: pov_pan
entries.description: A [pan](#pan) standing in for somebody looking around a space, usually with small hesitations and corrections in it. Add [point_of_view_shot](#point_of_view_shot) as well; use [following_pan](#following_pan) when the camera is holding on one subject instead of surveying.

entries.name: roll
entries.description: The camera rotates around the lens axis during the shot, so the horizon turns inside the frame. Tag [dutch_angle](#dutch_angle) when the frame is simply held at a slant with nothing rotating, and [spinning_camera](#spinning_camera) for a continuous turn.

entries.name: spinning_camera
entries.description: The [roll](#roll) keeps going for one or more complete turns, so the world revolves in frame. Distinct from [orbit_shot](#orbit_shot), where the camera travels around a subject and the background changes rather than merely tipping over.

entries.name: swing_pan
entries.description: The camera snaps from one subject to another and settles, often back and forth between two people. Faster than [slow_pan](#slow_pan) but stopping cleanly at each end, unlike [whip_pan](#whip_pan), which is about the blur in between.

entries.name: tilt_reveal
entries.description: A [tilt](#tilt) that ends on the thing the shot is about: up a building to its roof, or down a person from shoes to face. The vertical counterpart of [reveal_pan](#reveal_pan), and usually slow enough to be read as deliberate.

entries.name: nodal_pan
entries.description: A [pan](#pan) made about the lens's no-parallax point, so near and far objects do not shift against each other. Used for plates that must be stitched or composited; an ordinary tripod head always leaves a little parallax.

entries.name: remote_head_move
entries.description: The [pan](#pan) and [tilt](#tilt) are driven by a motorised remote head rather than a hand on the pan bar, giving moves that are faster, smoother or exactly repeatable. Common on cranes and vehicle rigs; the giveaway is unnaturally even speed.

entries.name: swish_tilt
entries.description: The vertical version of [whip_pan](#whip_pan): a [tilt](#tilt) fast enough to blur the frame into vertical streaks. Much rarer than the horizontal kind, and usually used to snap between a face and something well above or below it.

entries.name: handheld
entries.description: The camera is carried on the operator's hands or shoulder, so the frame breathes and drifts with their body. Use [gimbal_move](#gimbal_move) or [steadicam](#steadicam) when the wobble has been smoothed out, and [shaky_cam](#shaky_cam) when the instability is exaggerated on purpose.

entries.name: static_camera
entries.description: The camera stays put for the whole shot, usually on sticks or a clamp, and only the subject moves. Note that a static camera may still [pan](#pan) or [tilt](#tilt); tag locked_off framing here rather than under any travelling move.

entries.name: dolly_in
entries.description: The whole camera rolls forward toward the subject, so perspective changes and the background grows. Distinct from a zoom, where the lens tightens and perspective stays put; [push_in](#push_in) is the same move done slowly for emphasis.

entries.name: drone_shot
entries.description: The camera flies on a small remote aircraft, free to climb, orbit and skim close to the ground. Use [aerial_shot](#aerial_shot) for footage from a full-size helicopter or plane, which sits higher and moves in longer, flatter lines.

entries.name: follow_shot
entries.description: The camera trails a moving subject from behind or beside, holding it at a steady size in the frame. When the camera instead travels ahead of the subject and backs away from it, tag [leading_shot](#leading_shot).

entries.name: moving_camera
entries.description: The camera itself changes position during the shot, so the background shifts against the subject. The umbrella tag for any travelling move; use [static_camera](#static_camera) for the opposite. A [pan](#pan) or [tilt](#tilt) from a fixed spot does not count.

entries.name: push_in
entries.description: A slow, often barely visible creep toward the subject that tightens the frame over the length of a scene. Usually a [dolly_in](#dolly_in) taken at a crawl; reserve dolly_in for the ordinary, visible forward move.

entries.name: tracking_shot
entries.description: The camera travels alongside or with the action, classically on rails or a wheeled dolly. The general term for a lateral or accompanying move; use [dolly_in](#dolly_in) or [dolly_out](#dolly_out) when the travel is straight toward or away from the subject.

entries.name: aerial_shot
entries.description: The camera moves through the air above the landscape, shot from a helicopter, plane or stabilised nose mount. Reserve [drone_shot](#drone_shot) for the small unmanned rigs that can fly low and tight between obstacles.

entries.name: arc_shot
entries.description: The camera curves around the subject along part of a circle, so the background sweeps past while the subject stays framed. Use [orbit_shot](#orbit_shot) for a full turn around, and [trucking_shot](#trucking_shot) when the path is a straight line instead.

entries.name: crane_shot
entries.description: The camera rides an arm that lifts it high above or swings it out over the action, often rising off a close shot into a wide. A [jib_shot](#jib_shot) is the small version of the same idea; a straight vertical lift is a [pedestal_move](#pedestal_move).

entries.name: dolly_out
entries.description: The camera rolls backward away from the subject, opening the frame as it goes. Often ends a scene or exposes context; when the retreat is the point and the reveal lands at the end, tag [pull_back](#pull_back) or [moving_reveal](#moving_reveal) too.

entries.name: gimbal_move
entries.description: A motorised three-axis head holds the horizon while the camera is carried or driven through the space. The look is glassy and almost weightless, with none of the residual bob of [steadicam](#steadicam) or the shudder of [handheld](#handheld).

entries.name: moving_reveal
entries.description: The camera travels until something previously hidden comes into frame, often from behind a wall, a doorway or a foreground object. The move delivers information; [pull_back](#pull_back) is the specific case where retreating does the revealing.

entries.name: orbit_shot
entries.description: The camera circles all the way around the subject, which sits at the centre while the world revolves behind. Common from drones and gimbals; a partial sweep is an [arc_shot](#arc_shot).

entries.name: pull_back
entries.description: The camera withdraws from a tight frame to a wide one, usually to show where the subject actually is. The retreat carries the information; a plain [dolly_out](#dolly_out) is just the direction of travel without the payoff.

entries.name: shaky_cam
entries.description: Deliberately unsteady framing, jolting and re-finding the subject to suggest urgency or documentary immediacy. Tag [handheld](#handheld) for an ordinary carried camera; this one is for shake pushed past the point of comfort, whether shot or added later.

entries.name: slider_move
entries.description: A short rail, a metre or less, carries the camera through a small controlled glide. The everyday small-crew substitute for a dolly; use [tracking_shot](#tracking_shot) when the move covers real distance.

entries.name: steadicam
entries.description: A body-mounted stabiliser lets the operator walk, climb and turn while the frame floats free of their footsteps. Smoother than [handheld](#handheld) but with a slight human drift; a motorised [gimbal_move](#gimbal_move) is cleaner and stiffer still.

entries.name: trucking_shot
entries.description: The camera slides sideways, left or right, staying square to the subject rather than turning to follow it. Compare [arc_shot](#arc_shot), where the camera curves around the subject instead of running parallel to it.

entries.name: walk_and_talk
entries.description: Characters talk while walking and the camera travels with them, usually backing away ahead of them down a corridor. A staging convention rather than a rig; the underlying move is normally [leading_shot](#leading_shot) or [steadicam](#steadicam).

entries.name: camera_stabilized_in_post
entries.description: Wobble from a [handheld](#handheld) take has been smoothed by software, often leaving a slightly rubbery frame edge or warped straight lines. Worth separating from [steadicam](#steadicam) and [gimbal_move](#gimbal_move), where the steadiness was won on the day.

entries.name: floating_camera
entries.description: A slow drift with no obvious motivation, uncoupled from any subject, that keeps the frame quietly alive. Distinct from a purposeful [push_in](#push_in) or [follow_shot](#follow_shot): nothing in the scene is asking the camera to move.

entries.name: fly_over
entries.description: The camera passes directly above a subject or landmark and carries on beyond it, the ground sliding underneath. Compare [fly_through](#fly_through), where the camera threads a gap rather than clearing the top of something.

entries.name: fly_through
entries.description: The camera passes through a narrow opening — a window, an archway, a gap in the trees — without stopping. Usually a drone or a small gimbal rig; the momentary framing by the opening is what makes the shot.

entries.name: jib_shot
entries.description: A short counterweighted arm swings the camera up, down or across in one graceful sweep from a fixed base. The compact cousin of [crane_shot](#crane_shot); use that tag when the rig climbs storeys rather than a few feet.

entries.name: leading_shot
entries.description: The camera moves backward in front of a walking or running subject, keeping their face toward the lens. The mirror of [follow_shot](#follow_shot); the retreating operator is usually on a stabiliser or a pushed dolly.

entries.name: parallax_move
entries.description: A short lateral drift chosen so foreground objects slide visibly against the background, making the space read as deep. The move exists for the depth cue, not to follow anything; a plain sideways travel is a [trucking_shot](#trucking_shot).

entries.name: pedestal_move
entries.description: The camera rises or drops straight up and down on its column, keeping the lens level throughout. Not a [tilt](#tilt), which turns the head from one spot; not a [crane_shot](#crane_shot), which swings the camera out on an arm as it climbs.

entries.name: running_shot
entries.description: The operator runs with the subject, so the frame bounces on every stride and the background streaks. A more violent case of [follow_shot](#follow_shot); if the same energy is faked in a smooth rig or in post, use [shaky_cam](#shaky_cam).

entries.name: vehicle_mount
entries.description: The camera is clamped to a car, bike or train and moves because the vehicle does, whether pointed at the driver or out at the road. Tag this for the rig; a camera car chasing another vehicle is better tagged [tracking_shot](#tracking_shot).

entries.name: cable_cam
entries.description: The camera runs along a wire strung above the action, giving long smooth flights no dolly could manage. Familiar from stadiums and concerts; the path is fixed and straight, unlike the free flight of a [drone_shot](#drone_shot).

entries.name: dronie
entries.description: The camera starts close on a subject and flies up and backward at once, shrinking them into the landscape. A drone speciality and effectively an airborne [pull_back](#pull_back); on the ground the same idea is a [crane_shot](#crane_shot).

entries.name: motion_control_move
entries.description: A programmed rig repeats the identical camera path take after take, so passes can be layered or matched exactly. Tag it when the repeatability matters; an ordinary [crane_shot](#crane_shot) or [slider_move](#slider_move) driven by hand is not this.

entries.name: snorricam
entries.description: The camera is strapped to the performer's body facing back at them, so their head hangs still while the whole world lurches around it. Instantly recognisable and nearly always used for disorientation or intoxication.

entries.name: zoom_in
entries.description: The focal length lengthens during the shot, so the framing tightens without the camera going anywhere. Perspective stays flat and the background does not slide past the subject; when it does, the camera body moved and the shot is a push in rather than a zoom.

entries.name: rack_focus
entries.description: Focus is shifted mid-shot from one plane to another, handing attention from foreground to background or between two subjects. Both planes are sharp at some point in the take. Keeping a moving subject sharp instead is [follow_focus](#follow_focus).

entries.name: zoom_out
entries.description: The focal length shortens during the shot and the frame widens from a fixed position. Use it for the pull back that opens a scene out; if the camera itself retreats and the background changes shape, that is a pull out, not a zoom.

entries.name: digital_zoom
entries.description: The frame is tightened by cropping and scaling rather than by the lens, in camera or afterwards. Detail softens and grain grows as it goes, and the perspective never changes at all. An optical move is [zoom_in](#zoom_in).

entries.name: follow_focus
entries.description: The focus rides a subject as their distance from the camera changes, so they stay sharp throughout. Nothing else in frame is being handed off. Use [rack_focus](#rack_focus) when the point of the move is to transfer attention between planes.

entries.name: slow_zoom
entries.description: A zoom so gradual it is felt rather than seen, creeping in or out across a long take. Tag it when the move is meant to build unease or intimacy under dialogue; a zoom you can clearly watch happen is just [zoom_in](#zoom_in) or [zoom_out](#zoom_out).

entries.name: snap_zoom
entries.description: A single fast jab on the zoom ring, in or out, over a few frames. The middle of the move is a blur and the arrival is what reads. A snap zoom that lands hard on a close-up for shock or comedy is a [crash_zoom](#crash_zoom).

entries.name: zoom_out_reveal
entries.description: A zoom out whose point is the information it uncovers: the wider frame explains where the opening detail was. Tag it when the reveal is the reason for the move. A plain widening that reveals nothing new is just [zoom_out](#zoom_out).

entries.name: zoom_reframe
entries.description: A small correcting zoom made mid-take to tidy the framing, often while an operator also pans. It is housekeeping rather than expression, and it usually stops as soon as the composition is right, unlike the sustained move in [slow_zoom](#slow_zoom).

entries.name: aperture_pull
entries.description: The iris is opened or closed during the take, changing brightness and the depth of field together as it goes. Backgrounds go softer or firmer along with the exposure. If only the overall brightness matters, use [exposure_ramp](#exposure_ramp).

entries.name: crash_zoom
entries.description: A violent zoom straight into a face or object, usually with an audio hit on the landing. It is the loudest member of the [snap_zoom](#snap_zoom) family and almost always inward; a quick outward jab is better tagged snap_zoom alone.

entries.name: dolly_zoom
entries.description: The camera tracks in while the lens zooms out, or the reverse, keeping the subject the same size while the background stretches or compresses behind them. The giveaway is a stable subject with a warping background; a background that simply gets bigger is a plain [zoom_in](#zoom_in).

entries.name: exposure_ramp
entries.description: Brightness is ridden across a shot to hold an image while the light changes, typically walking from a dark interior into daylight. The result is a shot with no blown or crushed half. When the depth of field visibly moves with it, tag [aperture_pull](#aperture_pull).

entries.name: focus_breathing
entries.description: The framing swells or shrinks slightly as focus is changed, because the lens shifts its effective focal length. It looks like an accidental tiny zoom riding along with a pull. Note it as a lens artefact, not as a deliberate [zoom_reframe](#zoom_reframe).

entries.name: focus_hunting
entries.description: Autofocus searching back and forth, the image pumping in and out of sharpness before it settles. A visible mistake rather than a chosen move; a clean deliberate shift between planes is [rack_focus](#rack_focus).

entries.name: focus_in
entries.description: The shot opens out of focus and resolves to sharp, a soft blur settling into an image. Often used to start a scene or come out of a dream. The opposite ending, sharp drifting to blur, is [focus_out](#focus_out).

entries.name: focus_out
entries.description: The shot is racked away from any subject into soft blur, usually to end a scene or hide a cut. Nothing in frame is sharp by the end. A shot that begins blurred and clears is [focus_in](#focus_in).

entries.name: zoom_burst
entries.description: The zoom is moved during the exposure itself, so the frame smears outward from the centre in radial streaks. The subject core stays readable while the edges stretch. Distinct from the sharp frames of a fast [snap_zoom](#snap_zoom).

entries.name: zoom_during_move
entries.description: A zoom laid over a [pan](#pan), [tilt](#tilt) or track, so the framing changes by lens and by body at once. Tag it when both are clearly happening and neither cancels the other; when they do cancel and the background warps, it is a [dolly_zoom](#dolly_zoom).

entries.name: lens_tilt
entries.description: A tilting lens is swung during the shot, sliding the plane of focus across the scene at an angle instead of parallel to the sensor. Sharpness travels diagonally through the frame. A straight front-to-back shift is [rack_focus](#rack_focus).

entries.name: stepped_zoom
entries.description: A zoom taken in discrete jumps rather than one continuous move, so the frame ratchets closer in stages. Often done by cutting between focal lengths or by stopping the ring repeatedly. Distinct from a smooth pass of [zoom_in](#zoom_in).

entries.name: eye_level
entries.description: The lens sits at about the height of the subject's eyes and points straight across, so nobody is looked up at or down on. The neutral default; reach for [high_angle](#high_angle) or [low_angle](#low_angle) only when the [tilt](#tilt) is actually visible in the picture.

entries.name: high_angle
entries.description: The camera is above the subject and looks down, foreshortening the body and setting the figure small against the ground. For the extreme straight-down version use [overhead_shot](#overhead_shot), or [bird's_eye_view](#bird's_eye_view) when the whole place is laid out below.

entries.name: low_angle
entries.description: The camera is below the subject and looks up, so the figure looms and the background gives way to ceiling or sky. Use [worm's_eye_view](#worm's_eye_view) for the extreme taken from the ground looking nearly straight up.

entries.name: over_the_shoulder
entries.description: The camera sits behind and beside one person, whose shoulder and the back of the head fill a foreground corner while the other person faces the lens. The staple of dialogue coverage; its answering setup is the [reverse_angle](#reverse_angle).

entries.name: bird's_eye_view
entries.description: A steep view from far above, high enough that people and vehicles read as marks on a plan of the ground. Distinct from [overhead_shot](#overhead_shot), which points straight down from close range over one subject.

entries.name: crooked_horizon
entries.description: The horizon or the building lines lean a few degrees with no intent behind it — the camera simply was not level. Tag [dutch_angle](#dutch_angle) instead when the [tilt](#tilt) is strong and clearly meant.

entries.name: dutch_angle
entries.description: The camera is rolled so horizon and verticals run diagonally, deliberately, to unsettle the frame. Reserve it for the intentional expressive [tilt](#tilt); a mild slant nobody meant is [crooked_horizon](#crooked_horizon).

entries.name: frontal_angle
entries.description: The camera faces the subject head on and square to the front, both sides of the face or the facade equally visible. Its neighbours are [three_quarter_angle](#three_quarter_angle) for the turned view and [profile_shot](#profile_shot) for the full side.

entries.name: overhead_shot
entries.description: The camera is directly over the subject pointing straight down, so the floor or tabletop becomes the background and figures read as shapes. Use [bird's_eye_view](#bird's_eye_view) when the height is such that a street or landscape is spread out instead.

entries.name: point_of_view_shot
entries.description: The lens stands in for a character's eyes: we see what they see, from their height, sometimes with their hands or feet entering the bottom of the frame. Use [over_the_shoulder](#over_the_shoulder) when the person is still in front of the camera rather than behind it.

entries.name: profile_shot
entries.description: The subject is seen from directly to the side, the face or figure a full silhouette against the background. Turn a little towards the lens and it becomes [three_quarter_angle](#three_quarter_angle) instead.

entries.name: rear_angle
entries.description: The camera is behind the subject, who faces away into the scene, so we read the back of the head, the shoulders and the direction of travel. Use [over_the_shoulder](#over_the_shoulder) when a second person is being watched past that back.

entries.name: reverse_angle
entries.description: The answering setup, taken from roughly the opposite side of the action, so we now face the person we had been standing behind. It only means anything as the counterpart of an earlier angle; add [over_the_shoulder](#over_the_shoulder) when a shoulder fills the foreground.

entries.name: selfie_angle
entries.description: Shot at arm's length by the person in the picture, usually from slightly above the face and tilted down, often with the arm or the phone in frame. Distinct from a plain [high_angle](#high_angle) in that the subject is holding the camera.

entries.name: three_quarter_angle
entries.description: The subject is turned partway from the camera so one side of the face, or one corner of an object, leads — the everyday flattering portrait placement. It sits between [frontal_angle](#frontal_angle) and [profile_shot](#profile_shot); from behind it is [rear_three_quarter](#rear_three_quarter).

entries.name: chest_level
entries.description: Lens at about chest height, tilted mildly up at a standing figure. Typical of a camera carried at the body rather than raised to the eye; if the upward [tilt](#tilt) is pronounced, tag [low_angle](#low_angle) instead.

entries.name: down_the_barrel
entries.description: The subject looks straight into the lens and addresses the viewer, eyes on the camera axis. This is about where the gaze goes, not where the camera stands; a gaze aimed just past the lens is [off_axis_angle](#off_axis_angle).

entries.name: flat_lay
entries.description: Objects arranged on a plain surface and photographed straight down, edges squared to the frame. More a styling convention than a vantage: the picture is an [overhead_shot](#overhead_shot) of a deliberate layout rather than of a scene.

entries.name: ground_level
entries.description: The camera sits on the floor, road or grass, so the surface runs across the bottom of the frame in steep perspective. This is about camera height, not [tilt](#tilt) — a ground-level camera can still point level rather than up as in [worm's_eye_view](#worm's_eye_view).

entries.name: hip_level
entries.description: Camera held or mounted at waist height, looking up at people and lending them a little stature. Also the candid snapshot position, where the photographer never lifted the camera to the eye at all.

entries.name: objective_shot
entries.description: The camera observes from a position no character occupies, watching the scene from outside instead of through anyone's eyes. Worth tagging mainly where it stands against [point_of_view_shot](#point_of_view_shot) material in the same set.

entries.name: off_axis_angle
entries.description: The camera sits a little to one side of the subject's line of sight, so they look past the lens at an unseen interviewer. The standard interview placement, and the opposite choice from [down_the_barrel](#down_the_barrel).

entries.name: rear_three_quarter
entries.description: Seen from behind and to one side, so the back and one flank read together — the standard angle on cars and on a figure walking away. Use [rear_angle](#rear_angle) when the camera is squarely behind instead.

entries.name: shoulder_level
entries.description: The camera sits a little under the eyes, roughly at the subject's shoulders, so the face reads just above the lens. Still close to neutral; use [eye_level](#eye_level) when the drop is not readable in the frame.

entries.name: surveillance_angle
entries.description: The high, wide, corner-mounted vantage of a fixed security camera, looking down on a room or forecourt from near the ceiling with everything stretched at the edges. Tag plain [high_angle](#high_angle) when the placement has none of that fixed-camera character.

entries.name: worm's_eye_view
entries.description: Taken from the ground looking almost straight up, so walls, trees or a standing figure tower over the lens and converge overhead. The extreme end of [low_angle](#low_angle); keep low_angle for a merely raised chin.

entries.name: fifty_fifty_shot
entries.description: Two people face each other in profile, one on each side of the frame, the camera square to the line between them. A single symmetrical setup rather than a pair of [over_the_shoulder](#over_the_shoulder) and [reverse_angle](#reverse_angle) setups.

entries.name: knee_level
entries.description: The lens is at about knee height, well under a standing figure but not down on the floor. It sits between [hip_level](#hip_level) and [ground_level](#ground_level); pick ground_level when the camera is actually resting on the surface.

entries.name: raking_angle
entries.description: The camera looks along a line of things — columns, desks, a row of parked cars — rather than across it, so they stack into depth and shrink away. An oblique placement chosen for perspective, not a [roll](#roll) of the frame like [dutch_angle](#dutch_angle).

entries.name: upside_down_shot
entries.description: The frame is fully inverted, whether the camera was turned over or the picture rotated: sky along the bottom, figures hanging from the top edge. Always deliberate, and not to be confused with the partial [roll](#roll) of [dutch_angle](#dutch_angle).

entries.name: shallow_focus
entries.description: A thin plane of sharpness with everything in front and behind falling soft, usually the eyes sharp and the room dissolved. The blur rendering itself is [bokeh](#bokeh); the opposite is [deep_focus](#deep_focus).

entries.name: bokeh
entries.description: The character of the out-of-focus areas: how highlights render, whether the blur is creamy or busy. Tag it when the blur itself is a feature; the thin plane of sharpness that produces it is [shallow_focus](#shallow_focus).

entries.name: lens_flare
entries.description: A bright source striking the front element and scattering: streaks, arcs or coloured blobs across the frame. Chains of small repeated shapes are [lens_ghosting](#lens_ghosting); a horizontal blue streak is [anamorphic_flare](#anamorphic_flare).

entries.name: wide_lens_look
entries.description: A short focal length: near things loom, the background races away, and the room feels bigger than it is. About the optical character, not how much of the scene fits in frame, which is a shot size question.

entries.name: anamorphic
entries.description: Shot through a lens that squeezes a wide field onto the sensor and is unsqueezed afterwards, so the frame is wide, the [bokeh](#bokeh) is oval and highlights streak sideways. Tag the lens character here; the streak itself is [anamorphic_flare](#anamorphic_flare) and the stretched blur is [oval_bokeh](#oval_bokeh).

entries.name: bokeh_balls
entries.description: Defocused point lights rendered as distinct discs, typically city lights, fairy lights or sun through leaves behind the subject. If the discs are stretched sideways use [oval_bokeh](#oval_bokeh), if edged use [polygonal_bokeh](#polygonal_bokeh).

entries.name: deep_focus
entries.description: Near and far both readable at once, a face in the foreground and action at the back of the room equally crisp. Use it when the depth is clearly deliberate staging, not just a bright day with a small aperture.

entries.name: lens_compression
entries.description: Foreground and background stacked flat against each other, a far building sitting right behind a face. The perspective effect of shooting long from a distance; use [long_lens_look](#long_lens_look) for the general telephoto character.

entries.name: long_lens_look
entries.description: A telephoto focal length: a narrow slice of the scene, backgrounds pulled forward and thrown soft, the camera clearly standing back. If what you mean is specifically flattened distance between planes, use [lens_compression](#lens_compression).

entries.name: spherical_lens
entries.description: An ordinary undistorted-aspect lens: round [bokeh](#bokeh), flares that [bloom](#bloom) rather than streak, no horizontal stretch. Worth tagging mainly to say a picture is deliberately not [anamorphic](#anamorphic).

entries.name: vignetting
entries.description: Corners darker than the centre, from the lens itself, a matte box or a filter stack. Tag the visible falloff whatever made it; a hard black arc at one corner is usually a mechanical obstruction.

entries.name: vintage_lens_look
entries.description: Old glass character: low contrast, flare at the slightest provocation, soft corners, warm or greenish cast and busy blur. Use it for the overall optical signature; name the specific trait as well when one dominates.

entries.name: wide_angle_distortion
entries.description: Faces and objects stretched near the frame edges, a nose or a hand pushed comically large by being close to a short lens. Optical curvature of straight lines is [barrel_distortion](#barrel_distortion); extreme curved-field lenses are [fisheye](#fisheye).

entries.name: anamorphic_flare
entries.description: A long horizontal streak, usually blue, thrown across the frame by a light source. The most recognisable [anamorphic](#anamorphic) tell; a soft round [bloom](#bloom) around a lamp is not this.

entries.name: barrel_distortion
entries.description: Straight lines bowing outward toward the corners, most visible on horizons, doorframes and walls. A lens fault or character trait; if the whole frame curves into a circle-ish view it is [fisheye](#fisheye) instead.

entries.name: bloom
entries.description: Bright areas spilling a halo into their surroundings, so a window or a bare lamp glows outward into the frame. From the lens or a filter rather than the grade; a deliberate softening across the whole picture is [diffusion_filter](#diffusion_filter).

entries.name: chromatic_aberration
entries.description: Coloured fringes, typically magenta and green, along high-contrast edges and toward the frame corners. An optical fault; coloured haloes around bright sources spreading in every direction are [bloom](#bloom) instead.

entries.name: clinical_lens_look
entries.description: Modern glass shot for maximum cleanliness: edge-to-edge sharpness, neutral colour, flat field, no flare or fringing. The deliberate opposite of [vintage_lens_look](#vintage_lens_look), worth tagging when the sterility is the point.

entries.name: defocused_shot
entries.description: The whole frame is out of focus on purpose, shapes reduced to soft coloured masses. Different from [shallow_focus](#shallow_focus), where something is still sharp; often used for abstract inserts or a transition into a scene.

entries.name: diffusion_filter
entries.description: Glass or net in front of the lens taking the edge off contrast and blooming the highlights, keeping detail while softening the look. Sharper than [soft_focus](#soft_focus), which blurs the image outright.

entries.name: dirty_lens
entries.description: Rain, spray, dust, fingerprints or grease on the front element, smearing highlights and hazing the picture. Often left in on purpose for immediacy; the milky contrast loss on its own is [veiling_glare](#veiling_glare).

entries.name: fisheye
entries.description: An extremely wide curved-field view: the horizon bends hard, verticals bow, and the world seems wrapped around a bubble. Stronger and more obviously curved than plain [wide_angle_distortion](#wide_angle_distortion).

entries.name: large_format_look
entries.description: A big imaging area used wide: shallow focus at a wide field of view, so the subject sits close and detached while the whole room is still in frame. Not the same as a plain long lens, which narrows the view to get the same blur.

entries.name: lens_ghosting
entries.description: Repeated faint shapes of the light source marching across the frame, mirrored about the centre, caused by reflections between elements. A subset of flare worth its own tag when the ghost chain is the visible feature.

entries.name: macro_cinematography
entries.description: Filming very small subjects at near life size, where depth of field is millimetres and texture becomes landscape. About the optical setup rather than framing tightness; a face filling the frame is a shot size, not this.

entries.name: oval_bokeh
entries.description: Out-of-focus highlights squashed into vertical ovals, the signature of an [anamorphic](#anamorphic) taking lens. Round discs are [bokeh_balls](#bokeh_balls); a rotating swirl toward the edges is [swirly_bokeh](#swirly_bokeh).

entries.name: soft_focus
entries.description: The whole frame is gently unsharp while still clearly readable, a dreamy portrait softness rather than a mistake. If nothing is legible use [defocused_shot](#defocused_shot); if the softening is only in the highlights use [diffusion_filter](#diffusion_filter).

entries.name: through_glass
entries.description: Shot through a window, a bottle, a mirror or a sheet of plastic, so reflections, warping and colour ride over the subject. About what sits in front of the lens, not the subject being behind glass in the story.

entries.name: veiling_glare
entries.description: A wash of light over the whole image that lifts the blacks and drains contrast, from a source just outside the frame or an unshaded lens. No distinct streak or ghost, only milkiness; if shapes are visible use [lens_flare](#lens_flare).

entries.name: wide_open_aperture
entries.description: Shot at or near the lens's widest stop: paper-thin focus, soft corners, glowing highlights, often a little haze on contrast. Tag it when the wide-open character shows, not merely because the light was low.

entries.name: free_lensing
entries.description: The lens is held off the mount and tilted by hand, so focus smears across the frame and light leaks in at the gap. Rougher and more unstable than [tilt_shift_lens](#tilt_shift_lens), which does the same thing mechanically.

entries.name: polygonal_bokeh
entries.description: Defocused highlights come out as hexagons or pentagons because the iris was stopped down and its blades show. Use [bokeh_balls](#bokeh_balls) when the discs are round.

entries.name: probe_lens
entries.description: A long thin tube lens that pushes into tight spaces and focuses within centimetres, holding wide deep views inside a glass, a model or a mouth. Distinguished from [macro_cinematography](#macro_cinematography) by the impossible vantage point, not just the closeness.

entries.name: split_diopter
entries.description: A half lens element held over part of the frame so a very near subject and a far one are both sharp, with a soft seam running between them. Look for the tell-tale blurred dividing line; without it, use [deep_focus](#deep_focus).

entries.name: streak_filter
entries.description: A filter that draws lines out of point lights, either one long streak or a star with several points. The streaks appear on every bright source, unlike a flare, which comes from one direction.

entries.name: swirly_bokeh
entries.description: The background blur curls around the subject, discs smearing into arcs toward the frame edges. A trait of old uncoated portrait glass; tag alongside [vintage_lens_look](#vintage_lens_look) when the rest of the picture agrees.

entries.name: tilt_shift_lens
entries.description: The focus plane is tilted off perpendicular, laying a band of sharpness across the frame at an angle, or the lens is shifted to keep verticals straight. The miniature-looking version applies mostly to high views of real places.

entries.name: available_light
entries.description: Shot with whatever light was already there and no units added — room lamps, shop windows, daylight. Often uneven and mixed in colour. Use [natural_light](#natural_light) when that existing light is specifically the sun or sky.

entries.name: backlit
entries.description: The main source is behind the subject and facing the camera, so the front is in shadow and the edges glow. Describes the picture; [back_light](#back_light) names the fixture. If the shape goes fully black and featureless, use [silhouette_lighting](#silhouette_lighting).

entries.name: golden_hour
entries.description: The hour after sunrise or before sunset: warm low sun, long shadows, easy [backlit](#backlit) edges. Once the sun is below the horizon and everything goes cool and shadowless, use [blue_hour](#blue_hour).

entries.name: hard_light
entries.description: A small or distant source: shadow edges are crisp, texture is raised, specular highlights are tight. Bare sun, a bare bulb, a [spotlight](#spotlight). The opposite quality is [soft_light](#soft_light), and bouncing or diffusing a hard source turns it into one.

entries.name: key_light
entries.description: The dominant lamp, the one casting the shadow you actually read on the face. Its position is what names most of the portrait patterns — [rembrandt_lighting](#rembrandt_lighting), [split_lighting](#split_lighting), [butterfly_lighting](#butterfly_lighting). Use [fill_light](#fill_light) for the softer lamp that opens those shadows up.

entries.name: low_key
entries.description: Most of the frame sits in shadow with small controlled pools of light, so contrast is high and the darks are genuinely dark. Noir, horror, night interiors. Where the light and dark masses are sculpted for drama, also tag [chiaroscuro](#chiaroscuro).

entries.name: natural_light
entries.description: Sun, sky or moon doing the lighting, whether direct or bounced, with no artificial units in play. Distinct from [available_light](#available_light), which covers any pre-existing source including room lamps and signs.

entries.name: practical_light
entries.description: A lamp, bulb, sign, candle or screen visible in the shot that actually lights the scene. The fixture is part of the set dressing. If the apparent source is in frame but the real light comes from outside it, that is [motivated_lighting](#motivated_lighting).

entries.name: soft_light
entries.description: A large source relative to the subject: shadow edges fade gradually, skin looks smooth, highlights are broad. Overcast sky, a big diffusion frame, a wall bounce. If shadows have a hard cut instead, tag [hard_light](#hard_light).

entries.name: three_point_lighting
entries.description: The standard interview and dialogue setup: a [key_light](#key_light) to one side, a [fill_light](#fill_light) opposite it, and a [back_light](#back_light) separating the figure from the background. Tag it when you can read all three on the subject; a single lamp with a bounce card is [single_source_lighting](#single_source_lighting).

entries.name: atmospheric_haze
entries.description: Smoke, fog or hazer in the air so light has body: beams read, backgrounds go milky, contrast falls with distance. Where the haze resolves into distinct beams, tag [light_shaft](#light_shaft) as well.

entries.name: back_light
entries.description: A lamp behind the subject aimed at its back, drawing a bright edge that lifts it off the background. The fixture, not the effect: for the thin bright outline itself use [rim_light](#rim_light), and for a subject shooting into a source use [backlit](#backlit).

entries.name: blue_hour
entries.description: Twilight after sunset or before sunrise: an even cool blue sky, no direct sun, practicals starting to read against it. Warm low sun means [golden_hour](#golden_hour) instead.

entries.name: bounced_light
entries.description: A lamp aimed at a ceiling, wall or white card so the subject is lit by the reflection. Gives [soft_light](#soft_light) with a wrap that comes from the surface, not the fixture, and often picks up that surface's colour.

entries.name: coloured_gel
entries.description: A coloured filter on a lamp, so the light itself arrives blue, magenta or amber rather than the colour being added afterwards. Look for a coloured edge on a neutral face. Signs and tubes in frame are [neon_lighting](#neon_lighting).

entries.name: dappled_light
entries.description: Broken sunlight through leaves or a lattice, scattering soft-edged bright patches over the subject and moving with the wind. Natural and irregular, where [gobo_shadow](#gobo_shadow) is a deliberate pattern from a cut mask.

entries.name: fill_light
entries.description: The weaker source on the shadow side, lifting the dark half of the face so detail survives. Its strength against the key is the [lighting_ratio](#lighting_ratio). Taking it away entirely, or replacing it with black, is [negative_fill](#negative_fill).

entries.name: fluorescent_light
entries.description: Flat overhead strip lighting with a green or cold cast, no shadow direction to speak of, offices and corridors and shops. Reads institutional. Warm domestic bulbs are [tungsten_light](#tungsten_light).

entries.name: front_lighting
entries.description: The source sits beside the lens and hits the subject head on, so shadows fall behind it and the face flattens out. Little modelling, few texture cues. Move the source round and it becomes [side_lighting](#side_lighting).

entries.name: hard_shadow
entries.description: A sharp-edged cast shadow that is itself part of the composition — a figure's shadow on a wall, bars across a floor. Implies a [hard_light](#hard_light) source; use [gobo_shadow](#gobo_shadow) when the shape comes from a mask rather than the subject.

entries.name: high_key
entries.description: Bright, even, shadowless: pale backgrounds, low contrast, almost nothing in the dark end. Comedy, commercials, clean studio work. Judge it by the lighting scheme rather than by exposure — an overexposed [low_key](#low_key) shot is not this.

entries.name: light_shaft
entries.description: Visible beams cut through haze, smoke or dust — a window in a dark hall, a doorway, sun through trees. Needs something in the air to show the beam; the general haze without defined beams is [atmospheric_haze](#atmospheric_haze).

entries.name: mixed_colour_temperature
entries.description: Two or more sources of different colour in one shot — cool window against warm tungsten, green fluorescent against daylight — so faces carry two casts at once. Deliberate here, whether or not it was corrected.

entries.name: moonlight
entries.description: A cool, low, hard-edged wash standing in for the moon, usually blue and coming from one high side. In practice it is nearly always a lamp with a gel; where the whole scene is a daylight shot pushed cool, tag [day_for_night](#day_for_night).

entries.name: motivated_lighting
entries.description: Lamps placed so the light appears to come from something in the scene — a window, a lamp, a fire — even though the real source is off camera. Tag [practical_light](#practical_light) when the fitting itself is in frame and doing the lighting.

entries.name: neon_lighting
entries.description: Saturated coloured light from tubes and signs, usually several colours at once across faces and wet streets. Tag it for the look whether the signs are in frame or only their spill is; the coloured wash from a lamp with a filter is [coloured_gel](#coloured_gel).

entries.name: overcast_light
entries.description: Whole-sky diffusion: no visible shadow direction, gentle falloff, slightly cool colour. The natural version of a huge diffusion frame. Tag it for the condition; [soft_light](#soft_light) is the general quality it produces.

entries.name: rim_light
entries.description: A narrow bright line tracing the edge of a head or shoulder, separating it from a dark background. The visible result of a [back_light](#back_light) or [kicker](#kicker); when the whole body goes black against the source instead, use [silhouette_lighting](#silhouette_lighting).

entries.name: screen_glow
entries.description: A face lit by a phone, monitor or television: soft, close, usually cool or shifting in colour, and coming from below or straight on. Often paired with [flicker_lighting](#flicker_lighting) when the picture on it changes.

entries.name: side_lighting
entries.description: The source is roughly ninety degrees off the lens axis, so one side of the subject is lit and the other falls away. Strong texture and modelling. Taken to the limit, with a hard line down the nose, it is [split_lighting](#split_lighting).

entries.name: silhouette_lighting
entries.description: The subject is a flat black shape against a much brighter background, with no detail left in it. Distinct from [backlit](#backlit), where the front still holds some tone; here you read only the outline.

entries.name: single_source_lighting
entries.description: One lamp or window doing all the work, with no fill beyond what the room gives back. Shadows all fall the same way and there is only one set of catchlights — the tell that separates it from [three_point_lighting](#three_point_lighting).

entries.name: spotlight
entries.description: A tight hard beam picking out one subject and leaving the surroundings dark, with a readable edge to the pool. Stage and interrogation looks. A soft unbounded pool on a wall is [background_light](#background_light) instead.

entries.name: stage_lighting
entries.description: The theatrical or concert rig: coloured washes, hard front spots, haze in the beams, sources visible above the performers. Tag it for the whole scheme; a single isolating beam is [spotlight](#spotlight).

entries.name: street_light
entries.description: Night exterior lit by lamp posts: hard pools from above, deep gaps between them, often a strong orange or cold white cast. A common motivation for [top_lighting](#top_lighting) outdoors.

entries.name: tungsten_light
entries.description: Warm orange domestic and film-lamp light, roughly 3200K, going amber in the highlights and muddy in the shadows. Common as [practical_light](#practical_light) in interiors. The green-tinged office equivalent is [fluorescent_light](#fluorescent_light).

entries.name: window_light
entries.description: An interior lit by a window: soft and directional, falling off quickly across the room, often with a bright wall or curtain nearby. If the sun cuts straight through and lays a hard patch on the floor, tag [hard_light](#hard_light) too.

entries.name: background_light
entries.description: A lamp aimed past the subject at the wall or set behind it, often making a soft pool or gradient there. It shapes the backdrop, not the face — a light behind the subject aimed forward at them is [back_light](#back_light) instead.

entries.name: bare_bulb
entries.description: An unshaded bulb hanging in frame: a hard point source, hot in the picture, shadows radiating away from it in every direction. Cellars, garages, interrogation rooms. A shaded lamp is ordinary [practical_light](#practical_light).

entries.name: butterfly_lighting
entries.description: Key placed high and dead in front, giving a small symmetrical shadow under the nose and even cheeks. The glamour portrait pattern. Move the lamp off axis and you get [loop_lighting](#loop_lighting) or [rembrandt_lighting](#rembrandt_lighting).

entries.name: candlelight
entries.description: One or a few small flames close to the subject: a tiny warm pool, very fast falloff, everything past a metre in darkness. Softer and steadier than [firelight](#firelight), and almost always [practical_light](#practical_light).

entries.name: chiaroscuro
entries.description: Strong modelled contrast between light and shade, the figure carved out of darkness by one raking source. Painterly and deliberate; [low_key](#low_key) describes any dark scheme, while this one is about the shaping.

entries.name: day_for_night
entries.description: Shot in daylight and made to read as night: underexposed, cooled, sky held down, shadows still hard and sunlit if you look. Actually shooting after dark is [night_for_night](#night_for_night).

entries.name: eye_light
entries.description: A small source placed to put a catchlight in the eyes and keep them alive. Read it by the bright dot in the pupil rather than by any shadow it casts; it adds almost no exposure to the rest of the face.

entries.name: firelight
entries.description: Warm, low, flickering light from a fire, torch or brazier, usually from below and dropping off fast. Tag [candlelight](#candlelight) for the smaller, steadier single-flame version.

entries.name: flicker_lighting
entries.description: Light that changes level or colour within the shot — fire, a failing tube, a television, lightning, passing headlights. It is the instability that matters, not the source; note the source with [firelight](#firelight) or [screen_glow](#screen_glow) as well.

entries.name: gobo_shadow
entries.description: A patterned shadow thrown across the subject or wall by something in front of a hard source — blinds, a window frame, foliage cut-outs. If the pattern comes from real leaves in sunlight, [dappled_light](#dappled_light) fits better.

entries.name: hair_light
entries.description: A small lamp from above and behind putting a sheen on the top of the head. Narrower in aim than [back_light](#back_light), which lights the whole upper body edge; if it lands in the eyes rather than the hair it is an [eye_light](#eye_light).

entries.name: kicker
entries.description: A hard light from behind and off to one side, skimming the cheek or jaw at a raking angle. Lower and more sideways than a plain [back_light](#back_light), and usually the brightest thing on a face lit [low_key](#low_key).

entries.name: lighting_ratio
entries.description: How much brighter the key side is than the shadow side, from a nearly even face to one half in the dark. Tag it when the balance is the point of the picture; the extremes have their own tags, [high_key](#high_key) and [low_key](#low_key).

entries.name: loop_lighting
entries.description: Key slightly off axis and a little above, dropping a short nose shadow that loops down toward the corner of the mouth without touching the cheek shadow. The everyday portrait pattern, gentler than [rembrandt_lighting](#rembrandt_lighting).

entries.name: night_for_night
entries.description: Genuinely shot at night, lit by practicals and units placed for the dark, with real black in the gaps and no sky detail. The honest counterpart to [day_for_night](#day_for_night).

entries.name: rembrandt_lighting
entries.description: Key from about forty-five degrees and above, leaving a small lit triangle on the shadow cheek below the eye. If the cheek patch joins the lit side rather than standing alone, it is [loop_lighting](#loop_lighting).

entries.name: split_lighting
entries.description: Key at ninety degrees so the face divides down the middle, one half lit and one half dark. The hardest of the portrait patterns; if the shadow half still carries a lit triangle, tag [rembrandt_lighting](#rembrandt_lighting) instead.

entries.name: top_lighting
entries.description: Light coming straight down: bright forehead and cheekbones, eye sockets in shadow, a pool on the floor. Common under [practical_light](#practical_light) fittings and street lamps. Turn the source underneath instead and it is [underlighting](#underlighting).

entries.name: underlighting
entries.description: The source sits below the face and throws shadows upward, which reads unnatural and menacing. Usually motivated by a fire, a torch or a screen at chest height. The inverse of [top_lighting](#top_lighting).

entries.name: negative_fill
entries.description: Black cloth or board set close on the shadow side to take light away, deepening the modelling instead of adding a source. The picture reads contrasty and shaped with only one lamp visible. Adding light to that side is [fill_light](#fill_light).

entries.name: straight_cut
entries.description: One shot ends and the next begins on the same frame, with no [dissolve](#dissolve), fade or effect between them. The default join, and the tag for a cut whose only notable quality is that it is plain. If the join is meant to jolt, use [smash_cut](#smash_cut).

entries.name: continuity_editing
entries.description: Cutting that keeps screen direction, eyelines, positions and light consistent so the joins pass unnoticed. The default grammar of narrative work. Use it for the approach; the specific devices are [match_on_action](#match_on_action), [eyeline_match](#eyeline_match) and [shot_reverse_shot](#shot_reverse_shot).

entries.name: jump_cut
entries.description: A cut inside continuous action that skips a piece of it, so the subject snaps to a new position against an unchanged background. Deliberate in interviews and montages, an error elsewhere. A cut that hides the skip behind movement is [match_on_action](#match_on_action) instead.

entries.name: match_on_action
entries.description: The cut lands in the middle of a movement — a door swinging, an arm reaching — and the movement continues across it from a new angle. The travel hides the join. The opposite failure, where the movement restarts or skips, is a [jump_cut](#jump_cut).

entries.name: shot_reverse_shot
entries.description: A conversation cut back and forth between two opposing angles, each looking past the near shoulder at the other. The standard dialogue pattern. Keep both angles on one side of the axis, or you get [crossing_the_line](#crossing_the_line).

entries.name: cross_cutting
entries.description: Cutting back and forth between two or more lines of action in different places, so they read as happening at once or as a comparison. The chase and the rescue, the meeting and the wait. A single trip away from the action and back is a [cutaway](#cutaway).

entries.name: eyeline_match
entries.description: Someone looks off-screen and the next shot shows what they are looking at, from roughly where they were looking. The pairing is what makes the cut read; without the returning look on the subject it is a plain [cutaway](#cutaway).

entries.name: match_cut
entries.description: The two shots either side of the join are tied by something they share: a shape, a movement, a sound or a subject. The link carries you across a change of place or time. If the shared thing is purely compositional, use [graphic_match](#graphic_match).

entries.name: motivated_cut
entries.description: The cut is prompted by something inside the shot: a glance off-frame, a knock at the door, a hand reaching. The audience wants the next shot before it arrives. Cutting with no such prompt reads as arbitrary and belongs under [straight_cut](#straight_cut).

entries.name: smash_cut
entries.description: An abrupt join between two shots that clash — quiet to loud, calm to chaos, or the reverse — used for the jolt itself. Tag it only when the collision is the point; an ordinary unremarkable join is [straight_cut](#straight_cut).

entries.name: crossing_the_line
entries.description: The cut jumps to the far side of the imaginary axis between two subjects, so screen direction flips and they appear to swap sides or look the same way. Usually a mistake; deliberate when disorientation is wanted.

entries.name: cut_on_sound
entries.description: The picture changes exactly on a bang, a door, a downbeat or a word, so the sound covers the join. Different from [split_edit](#split_edit), where the two tracks deliberately cut at different moments rather than together.

entries.name: cut_to_black
entries.description: A hard cut from picture to an empty black frame, with no fade. Ends a scene or an act with a snap; often the sound stops with it or runs on alone. If the picture darkens gradually, that is a fade rather than a cut.

entries.name: elliptical_cut
entries.description: The cut leaves out the dull middle of an event: the character opens the car door, and is already at the desk. Storytelling by omission. It differs from [time_cut](#time_cut) in skipping a journey or process rather than sitting in one place.

entries.name: flash_cut
entries.description: A shot only a few frames long, gone almost before it registers, usually one of several in a burst. Used for shocks, memories and impacts. Distinguish from [jump_cut](#jump_cut), which is about the missing middle of an action rather than the length of the shot.

entries.name: graphic_match
entries.description: A [match_cut](#match_cut) made on form alone: a round window becomes a moon, a road becomes a scar. The two subjects have nothing to do with each other beyond the shape, colour or line that lands in the same part of the frame.

entries.name: hidden_cut
entries.description: A join disguised so the sequence reads as one unbroken take: the frame passes behind a pillar, goes dark, or is filled by a body. Tag the seam itself. For the smearing [pan](#pan) used the same way, use [whip_pan_cut](#whip_pan_cut).

entries.name: mismatched_cut
entries.description: A continuity error visible across the join: a cigarette changes hand, a glass refills, the light changes. Distinct from [jump_cut](#jump_cut), where the position is right but a piece of the action is missing.

entries.name: punch_in_cut
entries.description: A cut straight down the same axis to a noticeably tighter framing of the same subject, with no change of angle. Lands like emphasis. If the angle barely changes as well as the size, the result reads as a [jump_cut](#jump_cut).

entries.name: split_edit
entries.description: The picture and the sound cut at different moments, so one runs under the other for a beat. Smooths dialogue and carries a scene forward. Which one leads decides the tag: [j-cut](#j-cut) for sound first, [l-cut](#l-cut) for sound lingering.

entries.name: time_cut
entries.description: A cut that stays in the same place but moves the clock — the meal eaten, the room emptied, the light gone. The setting tells you time has passed without a [dissolve](#dissolve) or a title. Where the skip is short and inside one action, use [jump_cut](#jump_cut).

entries.name: whip_pan_cut
entries.description: A fast smearing [pan](#pan) runs into an equally fast pan on the next shot, and the cut hides in the blur. Common for jumping between locations at speed. If the join hides behind an object or darkness instead, that is the plain [hidden_cut](#hidden_cut).

entries.name: axial_cut
entries.description: Two or more cuts stepping in — or out — along the lens axis, each a jump nearer the same subject. Older and more mannered than a single [punch_in_cut](#punch_in_cut), which makes one step and stays there.

entries.name: intellectual_cut
entries.description: Two unrelated images joined so the collision states an idea — the speaker and the herd, the meal and the slaughter. The meaning lives in the join, not in either shot. Where the pairing links form instead of argument, use [graphic_match](#graphic_match).

entries.name: kuleshov_effect
entries.description: A neutral face cut against different objects appears to feel something different each time; the reading comes from the pairing, not the performance. Tag a cut built on that trick. Its cousin in argument rather than emotion is the [intellectual_cut](#intellectual_cut).

entries.name: overlapping_cut
entries.description: The opposite of a skip: part of the action is shown twice, once from each angle, so the moment stretches. Common in impacts and rituals. Contrast [match_on_action](#match_on_action), which continues the movement without repeating it.

entries.name: thirty_degree_rule
entries.description: Two shots of the same subject taken from angles too close together read as a nudge rather than a new view. Tag a cut that shows the fault, or one that pointedly ignores the convention. The related axis fault is [crossing_the_line](#crossing_the_line).

entries.name: dissolve
entries.description: One shot fades down while the next fades up, so both pictures are visible at once for a moment. The everyday soft transition between shots; if the outgoing picture goes to an empty colour first, tag [fade_out](#fade_out) or [fade_to_black](#fade_to_black) instead.

entries.name: fade_in
entries.description: The picture rises out of a flat colour, usually black, at the start of a scene or a film. Only the incoming shot is involved; when two shots overlap instead, use [dissolve](#dissolve).

entries.name: fade_out
entries.description: The picture sinks into a flat colour and the screen is left empty. Usually ends a scene or the film; [fade_to_black](#fade_to_black) and [fade_to_white](#fade_to_white) say which colour it landed on.

entries.name: fade_to_black
entries.description: A [fade_out](#fade_out) that ends on a black screen, the ordinary way to close a scene or a film. If the screen goes black in one frame with no ramp, that is [cut_to_black](#cut_to_black).

entries.name: fade_to_white
entries.description: A [fade_out](#fade_out) that ends on a blank white screen rather than black, often read as a [flashback](#flashback), a death or a dream. A single bright frame between two shots is [flash_frame](#flash_frame), not this.

entries.name: whip_pan_transition
entries.description: A fast smeared [pan](#pan) at the end of one shot is matched to another at the start of the next, so the blur hides the join. The camera has to be moving in both shots; a blur added afterwards is [blur_transition](#blur_transition).

entries.name: wipe
entries.description: A visible edge travels across the frame and the new shot follows behind it. The generic tag; use [iris_transition](#iris_transition), [clock_wipe](#clock_wipe), [checkerboard_wipe](#checkerboard_wipe) or the other named shapes when the edge is not a straight line crossing the frame.

entries.name: blur_transition
entries.description: The outgoing shot softens into blur and the incoming one sharpens out of it. Covers a rack to defocus in camera as well as a blur added in the edit; a directional smear from a moving camera is [whip_pan_transition](#whip_pan_transition).

entries.name: flash_frame
entries.description: One or a few blown-out frames sit between two shots, so the join reads as a blink or a camera flash. Much shorter than [fade_to_white](#fade_to_white), which ramps up and holds the empty screen.

entries.name: glitch_transition
entries.description: The join is covered by digital breakup: torn scanlines, blocky compression, colour channels pulled apart. A modern effect standing in for a signal fault; analogue tape damage between shots belongs here too.

entries.name: iris_transition
entries.description: A circle opens out of or closes onto the frame, the rest of the screen black. A silent-era device still used as a period flavour; a straight-edged [wipe](#wipe) is plain wipe.

entries.name: light_leak_transition
entries.description: A wash of orange or white light spills across the frame and the cut happens under it. Imitates light striking film in the camera back; the harder single-frame version is [flash_frame](#flash_frame).

entries.name: match_dissolve
entries.description: A [dissolve](#dissolve) between two shots holding the same shape or composition, so one form appears to become the other. The alignment is the point; an ordinary soft join is dissolve.

entries.name: morph_transition
entries.description: One picture is warped into the shape of the next so features slide and stretch across the join. Use it when shapes actually deform; if the two shots merely overlap, that is [dissolve](#dissolve) or [match_dissolve](#match_dissolve).

entries.name: object_wipe
entries.description: Something in frame passes close to the lens and fills it, and the cut happens while the screen is covered. A person, a car or a pillar does the work; nothing is added in the edit, unlike [wipe](#wipe).

entries.name: push_transition
entries.description: The incoming shot shoves the outgoing one off the frame, both pictures moving together. Different from [wipe](#wipe), where the old shot stays put while an edge crosses it.

entries.name: zoom_transition
entries.description: The frame punches in or out fast, usually with a smear, and the next shot is already there when it settles. A digital effect in most cases; if the shots were matched by a panning camera, use [whip_pan_transition](#whip_pan_transition).

entries.name: additive_dissolve
entries.description: A [dissolve](#dissolve) that brightens through the middle, the two shots adding up so the join blooms towards white before settling. Distinct from a plain dissolve, which holds an even exposure across the overlap.

entries.name: barn_door_wipe
entries.description: Two edges part from the centre or close towards it, like doors, letting the next shot through. A named [wipe](#wipe) shape; a single edge crossing the frame is plain wipe.

entries.name: checkerboard_wipe
entries.description: The new shot arrives in squares that fill in across the frame. One of the patterned video-switcher wipes; use [wipe](#wipe) when the edge is a single travelling line.

entries.name: clock_wipe
entries.description: The edge sweeps around the centre like a clock hand, revealing the next shot as it goes. A named shape of [wipe](#wipe); the circle growing from the middle instead is [iris_transition](#iris_transition).

entries.name: film_burn_transition
