entries.description: The frame appears to scorch and bubble away, going bright and then to the next shot. A film-damage flavour rather than a real optical device; for the softer wash use [light_leak_transition](#light_leak_transition).

entries.name: luma_wipe
entries.description: The new shot appears through a greyscale pattern, dark areas first, so the edge is ragged or textured rather than geometric. Common as ink, cloud or scratch transitions; a hard geometric edge is [wipe](#wipe).

entries.name: page_turn_transition
entries.description: A corner of the frame lifts and peels back like paper, showing the next shot underneath. A template effect, usually deliberately naive; for the flat sliding version use [push_transition](#push_transition).

entries.name: ripple_dissolve
entries.description: A [dissolve](#dissolve) with the picture rippling like disturbed water, the old shorthand for a memory or a dream beginning. Purely a period flavour now; a clean overlap is dissolve.

entries.name: spin_transition
entries.description: The picture rotates or tumbles away and the next shot arrives with it. One of the switcher and template effects, close kin to [push_transition](#push_transition); use [whip_pan_transition](#whip_pan_transition) when a real camera move carries the join.

entries.name: star_wipe
entries.description: A star-shaped hole opens onto the next shot. Almost always used as a joke or as a period stand-in for cheap video; for the plain moving edge use [wipe](#wipe).

entries.name: dialogue_scene
entries.description: A scene whose cutting is driven by who is speaking and who is listening, with the track of voices deciding the shape. The plainest sound relationship there is, and the natural home of [l-cut](#l-cut) and [overlapping_dialogue](#overlapping_dialogue).

entries.name: ambient_sound
entries.description: The continuous background of a place under everything else: wind, traffic, a crowd, air conditioning. It establishes where the scene is without pointing at any one source. For the bare recorded hush of an empty room, use [room_tone](#room_tone).

entries.name: diegetic_sound
entries.description: Sound that exists inside the story world and could in principle be heard by the people on screen: footsteps, traffic, a radio, a slammed door. Score and narration that only the audience hears are [non_diegetic_sound](#non_diegetic_sound).

entries.name: music_cue
entries.description: A discrete piece of music that starts and stops at chosen points against the picture. Tag it where the entry or exit of the music is itself the event. A licensed song dropped in whole is a [needle_drop](#needle_drop).

entries.name: non_diegetic_sound
entries.description: Sound laid over the picture that nobody in the scene can hear: orchestral score, a narrator, a title-card whoosh. If the sound has a visible or implied source in the world, tag [diegetic_sound](#diegetic_sound) instead.

entries.name: voiceover
entries.description: A voice speaking over the picture without being part of the pictured moment: a narrator, a letter being read, an interview laid over cutaways. If the speaker is simply off frame in the same scene, that is [off_screen_sound](#off_screen_sound).

entries.name: cut_on_the_beat
entries.description: Cuts are placed on the pulse of the music, so the picture changes with the track. Common in montages, trailers and titles. Tag it when the rhythm of the music is visibly deciding where the joins fall.

entries.name: j-cut
entries.description: The sound of the next shot starts before its picture arrives, pulling the viewer into the new scene early. Common on scene openings, where a voice or a room is heard a beat before it is seen. Sound lingering past the cut is [l-cut](#l-cut).

entries.name: l-cut
entries.description: The picture cuts to the next shot while the sound of the outgoing one keeps running underneath it. Heard constantly in dialogue: a line finishes over the listener's face. Its mirror, sound arriving before its picture, is [j-cut](#j-cut).

entries.name: needle_drop
entries.description: An existing song used more or less as recorded, usually starting on a cut and carrying a sequence. Recognisable by having vocals and a shape of its own rather than being written under the scene. Composed underscore is [music_cue](#music_cue).

entries.name: off_screen_sound
entries.description: A sound from the scene whose source is outside the frame, pulling attention to space the camera is not showing: a voice from the next room, a car approaching. If the sound comes from outside the world altogether, use [non_diegetic_sound](#non_diegetic_sound).

entries.name: silence
entries.description: The track is deliberately emptied, so a moment plays with little or nothing under it. Used for shock, dread or relief after loudness. A brief cut to nothing mid-scene reads better as [sound_dropout](#sound_dropout).

entries.name: sound_bridge
entries.description: One sound carries across a cut or a scene change, holding two separate pictures together. Use it for the general case; when the overlap is specifically trailing or leading dialogue, [l-cut](#l-cut) and [j-cut](#j-cut) are the finer tags.

entries.name: source_music
entries.description: Music that plays from something in the scene: a car stereo, a band, a phone speaker. It usually sits behind the dialogue and takes the room's acoustics. Music only the audience hears is [non_diegetic_sound](#non_diegetic_sound).

entries.name: synchronous_sound
entries.description: Sound locked to a visible action, so the picture and the track agree frame for frame: a door closing, a hand on a piano, lips matching words. Its opposite, sound deliberately let loose from the picture, is [asynchronous_sound](#asynchronous_sound).

entries.name: asynchronous_sound
entries.description: Sound deliberately detached from what is on screen, so the track describes something the picture does not show. Used for irony, memory or dread. A mistake in sync is not this; a bridge across a cut is [sound_bridge](#sound_bridge).

entries.name: audio_flashback
entries.description: Sound from another time, usually a remembered line, plays over the present picture. The voice belongs to the world but not to this moment, which separates it from [voiceover](#voiceover) narration and from a plain [sound_bridge](#sound_bridge) across a cut.

entries.name: dubbed_dialogue
entries.description: Voices recorded apart from the shoot and laid onto the picture afterwards, whether to replace a bad take or to speak another language. Often audible as dialogue that sits too cleanly above the room and lips that do not quite agree.

entries.name: foley
entries.description: Everyday sounds performed and recorded to picture: footsteps, cloth, keys, a cup set down. Tag it where these small human sounds are noticeably built up rather than caught on set. Background beds are [ambient_sound](#ambient_sound).

entries.name: inner_monologue
entries.description: A character's unspoken thoughts heard on the track while their face stays silent on screen. A narrower case of [voiceover](#voiceover), tied to a person in the scene rather than a storyteller outside it.

entries.name: leitmotif
entries.description: A short musical figure that returns whenever a particular person, place or idea appears, so the sound names what the picture shows. Recognised by repetition across the piece rather than by any one appearance.

entries.name: overlapping_dialogue
entries.description: Speakers talk across one another so lines collide instead of taking turns. It makes a scene feel crowded or unrehearsed and rules out clean cutting between clean lines. Not the same as a line running over a cut, which is [l-cut](#l-cut).

entries.name: room_tone
entries.description: The faint characteristic hiss of a specific room, recorded so cuts and gaps in dialogue can be filled without an audible hole. It is what a scene sounds like when nothing happens; a richer, described background is [ambient_sound](#ambient_sound).

entries.name: sound_dropout
entries.description: The track falls away abruptly for a few seconds, often at an impact or a shock, sometimes leaving only a ringing tone or a muffled hum. Distinguished from [silence](#silence) by being a sudden hole rather than a quiet passage.

entries.name: sound_perspective
entries.description: Level and reverb change with distance and framing, so a voice in a wide shot sounds further away than the same voice in a close-up. A realism choice, not a viewpoint one; hearing as a character hears is [subjective_sound](#subjective_sound).

entries.name: stinger
entries.description: A short sharp musical or effect hit landing on a single moment, usually a reveal or a scare. It punctuates rather than accompanies; a passage of music with a shape of its own is a [music_cue](#music_cue).

entries.name: subjective_sound
entries.description: The mix is bent to one character's hearing: the room goes muffled, a heartbeat rises, one voice comes forward while the rest recede. Tag it where the track takes a point of view rather than reporting the scene evenly.

entries.name: wall_to_wall_music
entries.description: Music runs almost without a break, under dialogue and quiet passages alike, so the picture is carried on a continuous bed. Tag the treatment of the whole piece, not a single entry, which is a [music_cue](#music_cue).

entries.name: slow_motion
entries.description: Action plays slower than it happened, usually shot at a higher frame rate and played back at the normal one. Water, hair and impacts stretch out and stay sharp. If the slowing comes and goes within the shot, tag [speed_ramp](#speed_ramp) as well.

entries.name: fast_motion
entries.description: Action plays quicker than it happened, either undercranked in camera or sped up afterwards. Gestures get jerky and comic. Use [time_lapse](#time_lapse) instead when hours are compressed into seconds rather than a moderate speed up.

entries.name: freeze_frame
entries.description: One frame is held on screen while the film keeps running, stopping the action dead. Often used to end a scene or pin a face for a caption. A frozen moment the camera then travels around is [bullet_time](#bullet_time) instead.

entries.name: time_lapse
entries.description: Frames taken seconds or minutes apart and played back at normal speed, so clouds race and shadows swing across a wall. The camera usually sits still. If it travels a distance between frames, tag [hyperlapse](#hyperlapse).

entries.name: high_frame_rate
entries.description: The shot was recorded at more frames a second than it will be shown at, or is shown at an unusually high rate. It is the means behind most [slow_motion](#slow_motion); tag it when the capture rate itself is what you are describing.

entries.name: hyperlapse
entries.description: A [time_lapse](#time_lapse) where the camera is moved a step or more between frames, so the whole viewpoint travels through a street or a landscape at speed. Distinct from a time_lapse on a locked tripod and from an ordinary sped up walking shot.

entries.name: real_time
entries.description: The action plays at the rate it happened, one second of screen for one second of world. Tag it when the unbroken pace is the point, not simply because nothing was sped up; anything retimed belongs under [time_remapping](#time_remapping).

entries.name: reverse_motion
entries.description: The footage runs backwards, so smoke gathers and spilt things leap into the glass. Tag it for the played-backwards look however it was made. A forward run followed by its own reverse is [ping_pong_loop](#ping_pong_loop).

entries.name: seamless_loop
entries.description: The last frame carries into the first so the clip repeats with no visible join. Common for backgrounds, patterns and short social clips. If the return is achieved by running the footage backwards, tag [ping_pong_loop](#ping_pong_loop).

entries.name: shutter_angle
entries.description: How much of each frame's time the shutter is actually open, which sets how much blur a moving thing leaves. The usual half-open setting looks natural; a narrow one gives the hard, stepping look of a battle scene.

entries.name: speed_ramp
entries.description: The playback rate changes inside a single shot, sliding from normal into [slow_motion](#slow_motion) or whipping up into [fast_motion](#fast_motion). Tag it when the change is visible mid shot; a clip that is uniformly slow is only slow_motion.

entries.name: stop_motion
entries.description: Objects are moved a little and photographed one frame at a time, so they seem to move by themselves. Look for the faint pop between frames. Use [pixilation](#pixilation) when the things being posed are people.

entries.name: time_remapping
entries.description: The clip's speed was rewritten after the fact rather than set by the capture rate, at one value or on a curve. Use it for the retimed look in general; [speed_ramp](#speed_ramp) is the specific case of the rate changing during the shot.

entries.name: bullet_time
entries.description: Time is nearly stopped while the viewpoint travels around the subject, usually shot with a ring of cameras fired together. The give-away is a moving angle over a frozen or crawling action, unlike a flat [freeze_frame](#freeze_frame).

entries.name: cinemagraph
entries.description: A picture that is still except for one small area that moves and loops, steam off a cup or hair in the wind. The stillness is masked in, not filmed. A clip where everything moves gently is not one.

entries.name: day_to_night_time_lapse
entries.description: A [time_lapse](#time_lapse) that runs through sunset or sunrise, the exposure shifted gradually so the picture holds while the light drops by many stops. The tell is the sky changing colour and stars or lights arriving inside one clip.

entries.name: frame_interpolation
entries.description: Missing frames were invented to stretch or smooth a clip, by blending neighbours or by tracking motion between them. Look for smeared edges and warped limbs around fast movement. It is what betrays [slow_motion](#slow_motion) faked from ordinary footage.

entries.name: judder
entries.description: Movement arrives in visible steps rather than smoothly, typically a slow [pan](#pan) or a frame rate that does not divide into the playback rate. It is a defect of the motion itself, not the smearing that [frame_interpolation](#frame_interpolation) leaves.

entries.name: ping_pong_loop
entries.description: A short clip that plays forward then straight back again, over and over, so the ends always meet. The bounce is obvious once you watch a gesture undo itself. Use [seamless_loop](#seamless_loop) for a clip that loops forward only.

entries.name: super_slow_motion
entries.description: Extreme slowing from several hundred to several thousand frames a second, the range where a droplet or a bursting balloon becomes readable. Reserve it for that scale; ordinary sixty or hundred and twenty frame work is just [slow_motion](#slow_motion).

entries.name: go_motion
entries.description: Stop_motion in which the puppet is moved during each exposure, so every frame carries real blur and the result flows instead of strobing. Tag it only when that blur is visible; crisp frames mean ordinary [stop_motion](#stop_motion).

entries.name: motion_control_time_lapse
entries.description: A [time_lapse](#time_lapse) shot on a programmed slider or head that nudges the camera a fraction between frames, giving a perfectly smooth drift or [pan](#pan). Machine-even movement over a fixed distance, unlike the free travel of a [hyperlapse](#hyperlapse).

entries.name: pixilation
entries.description: Stop_motion done with live people, shot a frame at a time so they skate, vanish and fly. The bodies are real but the movement is impossible and twitchy. Not to be confused with pixelation, which is about blocky pixels.

entries.name: slit_scan
entries.description: Each column or row of the picture is recorded at a different instant, so movement smears into long streaks and straight edges bend. Made with a moving slit or a rolling scan rather than by blurring in post.

entries.name: step_printing
entries.description: Frames are repeated or dropped and printed with a long exposure, so movement steps forward in smeared jerks instead of flowing. A stuttering, trailing look; the smooth kind of slowing is plain [slow_motion](#slow_motion).

entries.name: variable_frame_rate
entries.description: The clip was recorded with the frame rate changing as it ran, or with a capture rate that does not match the timeline it sits in. It shows up as drifting sound and uneven motion until the footage is conformed.

entries.name: wagon_wheel_effect
entries.description: Something spinning fast appears to crawl, stand still or turn backwards, because each frame catches it near the same position. Spokes, rotors and rims are the usual suspects. A sampling illusion, not real [reverse_motion](#reverse_motion).

entries.name: landscape_orientation
entries.description: The frame is wider than it is tall, whatever the exact proportion. The default for nearly all moving pictures, worth tagging mainly to separate them from [vertical_video](#vertical_video) and [square_frame](#square_frame).

entries.name: sixteen_by_nine
entries.description: The standard broadcast and web [widescreen](#widescreen) shape at about 1.78:1. What a phone shoots held sideways and what most video players expect, so it fills a screen edge to edge with no bars. Slightly less wide than [flat_ratio](#flat_ratio).

entries.name: widescreen
entries.description: A frame noticeably wider than it is tall, anything past the old television shape. Use it as the general tag when you can see the picture is wide but cannot pin the exact number; reach for [flat_ratio](#flat_ratio), [sixteen_by_nine](#sixteen_by_nine) or [cinemascope](#cinemascope) when you can.

entries.name: four_by_three
entries.description: The old television and early digital shape, a third wider than tall. Boxy, with tall [headroom](#headroom) and no room at the sides; on a wide screen it shows as [pillarboxed](#pillarboxed). Distinct from [academy_ratio](#academy_ratio), which is a hair wider still.

entries.name: letterboxed
entries.description: Black bars along the top and bottom because the picture is wider than the screen it sits in. A property of the presentation, not of the shooting; if the bars are part of the picture file itself and cannot be removed, tag [faux_letterbox](#faux_letterbox) too.

entries.name: vertical_video
entries.description: A moving picture taller than it is wide, shot for a phone held upright, typically 9:16. Framing crowds in on faces and loses the sides of a room. Use [square_frame](#square_frame) for 1:1 and [pillarboxed](#pillarboxed) when a wide picture merely sits inside a tall screen.

entries.name: anamorphic_ratio
entries.description: A wide frame obtained by squeezing the picture onto a narrower negative or sensor and stretching it back on the way out, rather than by cropping. Use it when the wide shape is genuinely optical; use [cinemascope](#cinemascope) for the finished proportion alone.

entries.name: cinemascope
entries.description: The wide theatrical frame around 2.35 to 2.39:1, more than twice as wide as it is tall. On a television it leaves thick bars top and bottom. Tag [anamorphic_ratio](#anamorphic_ratio) as well only when the width came from a squeezed lens rather than a crop.

entries.name: cropped_frame
entries.description: The picture has been trimmed from its original shape, so heads sit tight to the edge or a composition looks cut off. Use it whenever the framing on screen is not the framing that was shot, and [pan_and_scan](#pan_and_scan) when the crop tracks the action.

entries.name: flat_ratio
entries.description: The common theatrical [widescreen](#widescreen) shape at about 1.85:1, shot with ordinary spherical lenses rather than squeezed. Only a little wider than [sixteen_by_nine](#sixteen_by_nine), so it shows thin bars on a television. The alternative to [cinemascope](#cinemascope) on a cinema screen.

entries.name: pillarboxed
entries.description: Black bars down the left and right because the picture is narrower than the screen, the usual fate of [four_by_three](#four_by_three) material on a wide display. The vertical counterpart of [letterboxed](#letterboxed).

entries.name: square_frame
entries.description: A true 1:1 picture, as tall as it is wide. Common in social crops and some art projects. Do not use it for [academy_ratio](#academy_ratio) or [four_by_three](#four_by_three), which only look squarish.

entries.name: academy_ratio
entries.description: The classic sound-era frame, very slightly wider than tall at about 1.37:1. Almost square to a modern eye but not quite; use [square_frame](#square_frame) only for a true 1:1, and [four_by_three](#four_by_three) for the television shape it is often confused with.

entries.name: european_widescreen
entries.description: The narrower continental theatrical shape at about 1.66:1, between [four_by_three](#four_by_three) and [flat_ratio](#flat_ratio). Common in older European and animated features; noticeably taller than [sixteen_by_nine](#sixteen_by_nine) when you put them side by side.

entries.name: faux_letterbox
entries.description: Bars burned into the picture itself to make an ordinary frame look cinematic, rather than bars added by the player. Tell them apart by whether the black moves with the image when it is cropped or scaled.

entries.name: hard_matte
entries.description: The wide shape is fixed at the camera or the lab, with the unused top and bottom blacked out for good. Nothing can be recovered outside it, unlike a [soft_matte](#soft_matte) frame, whose full height still exists on the negative.

entries.name: imax_ratio
entries.description: The tall large-format shape, near 1.43:1 or 1.90:1, which gains height rather than width against the surrounding scenes. Often seen as a frame that suddenly grows top and bottom mid-film; the switching itself is [variable_aspect_ratio](#variable_aspect_ratio).

entries.name: open_matte
entries.description: A version that shows the full exposed height instead of the intended wide crop, so there is more picture above and below and sometimes a stray light or rig edge. The opposite trade to [pan_and_scan](#pan_and_scan), which loses the sides instead.

entries.name: pan_and_scan
entries.description: A wide picture cut down to a narrow screen by choosing which part of the width to keep, panning within the original frame as the action moves. Loses the sides; [open_matte](#open_matte) instead adds height, and [letterboxed](#letterboxed) keeps the whole width.

entries.name: squeezed_frame
entries.description: The picture is still optically compressed and has not been stretched back out, so everything looks tall and thin, circles read as ovals. A mistake in presentation rather than a look; the corrected version is [desqueezed_frame](#desqueezed_frame).

entries.name: stretched_frame
entries.description: The picture has been pulled to fill a screen of the wrong shape, so faces are fat or thin and nothing matches its real proportions. A presentation fault, not a squeezed original; use [squeezed_frame](#squeezed_frame) for a picture that was never unsqueezed.

entries.name: variable_aspect_ratio
entries.description: The shape of the frame changes within one piece, the bars opening or closing between sequences. Usually marks a shift in time, scale or point of view. Tag the ratios involved as well when they are identifiable.

entries.name: desqueezed_frame
entries.description: A squeezed picture stretched back to its true proportions, the normal state of [anamorphic_ratio](#anamorphic_ratio) material once it is prepared for viewing. Worth tagging only where the raw and corrected versions sit side by side.

entries.name: overscan
entries.description: The outer edge of the picture is cut off by the display, or conversely the frame carries a border of material never meant to be seen. A television-era habit that leaves stray edges and half-visible bars in old transfers.

entries.name: soft_matte
entries.description: The full frame is exposed and the wide shape is only a marked-off area, so the picture outside it survives on the negative. That extra height is what an [open_matte](#open_matte) release shows.

entries.name: title_safe
entries.description: The inset area of the frame guaranteed to survive any crop or [overscan](#overscan), where text and important action are kept. Visible as a guide box in production frames rather than in a finished picture.

entries.name: ultra_wide_frame
entries.description: Wider still than [cinemascope](#cinemascope), roughly 2.55:1 and up, a long letterbox slot of a picture. Rare, usually a large-format or special-process release. Below about 2.4:1 use cinemascope instead.

entries.name: windowboxed
entries.description: Bars on all four sides, so the picture floats in the middle of the screen. Usually the result of [letterboxed](#letterboxed) material being [pillarboxed](#pillarboxed) again, or of a small file scaled into a large frame.

entries.name: cool_grade
entries.description: The frame tipped toward blue, cyan or steel across the board, a common shorthand for night, cold and clinical spaces. As with [warm_grade](#warm_grade) this is the colour applied afterwards, not the colour of the light that was there. Night shot in daylight and graded down is [day_for_night](#day_for_night).

entries.name: desaturated_grade
entries.description: Colour pulled down well below life without going all the way to grey, leaving muted greens, greys and dull skin. Common in war, crime and post-apocalyptic looks. If almost nothing is left use [monochrome_grade](#monochrome_grade); if colour is instead pushed up, [saturated_grade](#saturated_grade).

entries.name: warm_grade
entries.description: The whole frame tipped toward amber, gold or red after the fact, so highlights and shadows both carry the bias. Tag the finish, not the lamp: [firelight](#firelight) or a low sun on set belongs with the lighting tags. Use [color_cast](#color_cast) when the tint reads as a fault rather than a choice.

entries.name: clipped_highlights
entries.description: Bright areas driven flat to white with no texture in them — skies, windows, practicals reduced to blank shapes. May be a capture failure or a deliberate hot look. A gentle, gradual approach to white instead is [highlight_rolloff](#highlight_rolloff).

entries.name: color_cast
entries.description: An overall tint sitting on the whole picture where neutrals should be neutral — a green office, a magenta night, an orange mixed-light interior. Use it when the bias reads as uncorrected rather than styled; a chosen bias is [warm_grade](#warm_grade) or [cool_grade](#cool_grade).

entries.name: crushed_blacks
entries.description: Shadows pushed to solid black with no detail left in them, so dark areas read as flat holes in the frame. Often deliberate in a [high_contrast_grade](#high_contrast_grade). The opposite treatment, shadows raised off the floor, is [lifted_blacks](#lifted_blacks).

entries.name: film_emulation
entries.description: A digital picture graded to sit where a photochemical print would: rolled-off highlights, coloured shadows, a slight cast in the neutrals. Usually arrives with [film_grain_overlay](#film_grain_overlay) and [halation](#halation). Reserve it for the whole tonal impression rather than any one added artefact.

entries.name: film_grain_overlay
entries.description: Grain added in post over a clean digital image, sitting evenly across the frame including flat areas that would never have shown sensor noise. Look for grain that does not change with exposure. Digital sensor noise from a dark shot is a different thing entirely.

entries.name: flat_profile
entries.description: Low-contrast, low-saturation capture kept deliberately soft so it can be graded later — the whole picture sits in the middle greys. Different from [low_contrast_grade](#low_contrast_grade), which is a finished choice; this one looks unfinished. Log encodings specifically are [log_footage](#log_footage).

entries.name: high_contrast_grade
entries.description: Blacks driven down and highlights driven up, so the midtones thin out and the picture reads hard and graphic. Judge it on the finished tone curve, not the lighting ratio on set. Blacks alone going solid is [crushed_blacks](#crushed_blacks).

entries.name: lifted_blacks
entries.description: The darkest parts of the frame raised well off black so they sit grey and often tinted, the classic faded print or matte look. Look at the corners of a night interior to spot it. Pushed further into an overall haze it becomes [faded_film_look](#faded_film_look).

entries.name: log_footage
entries.description: Camera material still in its logarithmic capture curve: washed out, milky and slightly green or magenta, holding range for a grade that has not happened yet. Tag the state of the file, not a style. Any flat-looking low-contrast capture is [flat_profile](#flat_profile).

entries.name: low_contrast_grade
entries.description: Everything held into a narrow band of greys, soft and hazy, with neither a true black nor a clean white. Often paired with [lifted_blacks](#lifted_blacks) for a faded look. An untouched capture that looks this way straight off the camera is [flat_profile](#flat_profile), not a grade.

entries.name: monochrome_grade
entries.description: Colour taken out in finishing, leaving one tonal scale — grey, or tinted a single hue. Tag it for the decision made after shooting, so the frame may still show colour-derived contrast a true monochrome capture would not. Two hues split across the scale is [split_toning](#split_toning).

entries.name: saturated_grade
entries.description: Colour pushed hard, so reds, greens and blues read at full strength and skin can go ruddy. Typical of musicals, comedy and advertising work. The opposite end of the same knob from [desaturated_grade](#desaturated_grade); contrast on its own is [high_contrast_grade](#high_contrast_grade).

entries.name: teal_and_orange
entries.description: Skin pushed warm and orange while everything in shadow slides toward teal, the two ends of the picture pulled apart into complementary colours. Tag it when the split is visibly deliberate, not just a warm room against a blue window. A single overall bias is [warm_grade](#warm_grade) or [cool_grade](#cool_grade).

entries.name: ungraded
entries.description: Raw or straight-out-of-camera material with no colour work applied: mismatched shots, uncorrected white balance, whatever the sensor made of the room. Useful for marking dailies and reference frames apart from finished ones.

entries.name: vignette_grade
entries.description: Corners and edges darkened in post to pull the eye to the middle, usually a smooth oval falloff with no hard edge. Distinguish from real lens [vignetting](#vignetting), which is fixed by the optics and appears on every shot at that stop.

entries.name: bleach_bypass
entries.description: The silver-retention look: heavy contrast, gritty grain and colour drained almost out, as if a monochrome layer sat over the colour one. Skin goes pale and metallic. Distinct from a plain [desaturated_grade](#desaturated_grade) by how hard the blacks and whites are pushed.

entries.name: cross_processed
entries.description: Wrong-chemistry colour: shifted, clashing hues with a strong cast in one end of the scale and the other end skewed the other way, usually green-yellow highlights over cyan shadows. Tag it for the emulated look as much as the real process. A tidy warm/cool separation is [teal_and_orange](#teal_and_orange).

entries.name: dust_and_scratches
entries.description: Specks, hairs and vertical tramline scratches laid over the picture to suggest a worn print. Added deliberately in most modern work. For the colour side of aging — faded, milky, drifting hues — tag [faded_film_look](#faded_film_look).

entries.name: faded_film_look
entries.description: Washed, aged print: low contrast, weak colour, milky shadows and often a faint magenta or yellow drift, as though the stock had sat in the sun. Usually built from [lifted_blacks](#lifted_blacks) plus [low_contrast_grade](#low_contrast_grade). Physical damage on top of it is [dust_and_scratches](#dust_and_scratches).

entries.name: green_grade
entries.description: The frame pushed toward green or yellow-green, a shorthand for institutions, illness and menace. Skin turns sallow and whites go swampy. If the green looks accidental — a room full of fluorescent tubes nobody corrected — use [color_cast](#color_cast) instead.

entries.name: halation
entries.description: A soft red-orange bleed hugging bright edges — a window frame, a bulb, a white shirt against dark — imitating light scattering back through film base. Tag it when the glow is coloured and tight to the highlight. A neutral, wider spread is [bloom](#bloom).

entries.name: hdr_grade
entries.description: Graded for a high dynamic range display, so highlights sit far above diffuse white — specular hits, skies and practicals stay bright and coloured where a standard version would clip. Tag it for the delivery, not for a heavy tone-mapped still look.

entries.name: highlight_rolloff
entries.description: Highlights that ease gently into white, keeping colour and texture in a bright sky or a lit cheek instead of snapping off. A signature of [film_emulation](#film_emulation) and a good grade generally. Tag its absence as [clipped_highlights](#clipped_highlights).

entries.name: light_leak
entries.description: A wash of orange or red flooding in from one edge of the frame, imitating light reaching film through a bad seal. Almost always composited in afterwards, and it usually drifts or pulses across a shot. A burst that consumes the whole frame at a cut is [film_burn](#film_burn).

entries.name: selective_color
entries.description: One colour left in while everything else is taken to grey — a red coat, a yellow taxi — isolated with a key or a mask. Obvious and usually deliberate. Not to be confused with a [monochrome_grade](#monochrome_grade) that happens to include a bright object.

entries.name: sepia_grade
entries.description: Colour removed and the result tinted a single warm brown, the old-photograph treatment, often used to mark a [flashback](#flashback). One hue throughout; if a second colour sits in the shadows it is [duotone_grade](#duotone_grade) or [split_toning](#split_toning).

entries.name: split_toning
entries.description: Shadows tinted one colour and highlights another over an otherwise normal picture — cool shadows with warm highlights being the usual pairing. Milder than [duotone_grade](#duotone_grade). When the split is specifically orange skin against teal shadows, tag [teal_and_orange](#teal_and_orange).

entries.name: vhs_look
entries.description: Analogue tape finishing: smeared colour, tracking noise across the bottom, scan lines, chroma bleeding sideways off saturated edges. Usually applied to clean footage as a period or found-footage cue. Film-style aging instead is [dust_and_scratches](#dust_and_scratches) or [faded_film_look](#faded_film_look).

entries.name: duotone_grade
entries.description: The picture mapped onto two colours end to end, a poster-like look with no natural hue left anywhere. Stronger and flatter than [split_toning](#split_toning), which keeps a normal picture underneath and only tints the extremes.

entries.name: film_burn
entries.description: The frame blistering into white and orange as if the stock stopped in the gate and caught the lamp, typically used as a transition or a stress cue. Brief and total, where [light_leak](#light_leak) sits at an edge and lingers.

entries.name: gate_weave
entries.description: The whole frame drifting a little from side to side or up and down, as an unsteady film gate would move it, added in finishing along with grain. Look at a fixed edge in a locked-off shot. Camera unsteadiness from the operator is a movement tag, not this.

entries.name: end_credits
entries.description: The list of everyone who worked on the piece, scrolling or carded, at the end. Tag the credit passage itself, including any music-only tail; a scene tucked after it is a [post_credits_scene](#post_credits_scene).

entries.name: flashback
entries.description: A scene set earlier than the story's present, entered to show something that already happened. Tag the whole passage, not the join that leads into it; the join belongs with the transition tags.

entries.name: long_take
entries.description: A shot held far longer than the surrounding cutting rhythm, often a minute or more. Tag the shot itself, not the whole scene; if the entire scene runs without a cut, use [oner](#oner) instead.

entries.name: montage_sequence
entries.description: A run of short shots compressing time, travel or a process into a passage carried by music rather than dialogue. The unit is the sequence; a single unusual join between two shots belongs with the cut tags.

entries.name: title_sequence
entries.description: The designed opening passage carrying the name of the piece and the lead credits, usually with its own music and graphics. Tag the sequence as a whole; a single lettered card inside a scene is an [intertitle](#intertitle).

entries.name: action_sequence
entries.description: A passage carried by physical event rather than talk, shot for movement and cut fast. Use the narrower [chase_sequence](#chase_sequence) when it is a pursuit, and [set_piece](#set_piece) when the whole thing is staged as a showcase.

entries.name: b_roll
entries.description: Supporting footage of places, hands, objects or atmosphere laid over narration or an interview to carry a passage. Tag the material by its role in the piece; a single shot dropped in mid-scene is a [cutaway](#cutaway).

entries.name: closing_shot
entries.description: The last image before the picture ends or the credits start, often held longer than the shots around it. Pair with [opening_shot](#opening_shot) when the two deliberately echo each other, which is a [bookend](#bookend).

entries.name: cold_open
entries.description: A scene played before the titles, dropping the viewer straight into an incident. Different from an ordinary opening in that the [title_sequence](#title_sequence) follows it rather than preceding it.

entries.name: establishing_sequence
entries.description: Several shots at the head of a scene that place the viewer in a location before the action starts, working from wide to close. Use when it takes a run of shots; a single wide opener is an establishing shot.

entries.name: oner
entries.description: A complete scene played out in a single unbroken shot, blocking and camera choreographed to cover every beat. Stronger than [long_take](#long_take), which only says the shot was held; a oner has to carry the whole scene.

entries.name: opening_shot
entries.description: The first image of the piece, chosen to set tone and place before anything is explained. Use it for the frame that opens the whole work, not merely the first shot of any given scene.

entries.name: split_screen
entries.description: The frame divided into two or more panels showing different views at once, classically the two ends of a phone call. Use [picture_in_picture](#picture_in_picture) instead when one small inset sits over a full-frame image.

entries.name: act_break
entries.description: The seam where one act ends and the next begins, usually on a turn or a cliffhanger and often where a break falls. Tag the structural join, not the picture treatment used to reach it.

entries.name: bookend
entries.description: An opening and a closing that deliberately echo each other, the same place, framing or line returning at the end. Tag either half of the pair; it is a structural rhyme, not just a repeated setup.

entries.name: chapter_title
entries.description: A card naming a numbered or titled part of the piece, dividing it into sections. A specific use of the [intertitle](#intertitle), and worth its own tag when the whole work is built as chapters.

entries.name: chase_sequence
entries.description: A pursuit sustained across many shots, on foot, in vehicles or through a building, cutting between pursuer and pursued. A narrower case of [action_sequence](#action_sequence), tagged when the pursuit is the structure of the scene.

entries.name: credits_over_action
entries.description: Opening credits laid over the first scene rather than over dedicated graphics, so the story starts while the names are still arriving. The distinction from an ordinary [title_sequence](#title_sequence) is that the drama has already begun.

entries.name: dream_sequence
entries.description: A passage presented as a dream, vision or hallucination rather than events in the story's world, often marked by odd light, sound or logic. Unlike a [flashback](#flashback) it need not have happened at all.

entries.name: epilogue
entries.description: A short closing passage after the main story has resolved, showing how things settled, often after a time jump. Comes before the credits; a scene after them is a [post_credits_scene](#post_credits_scene).

entries.name: flashforward
entries.description: A scene from later than the story's present, shown early as a glimpse of what is coming. The mirror of [flashback](#flashback), and worth separating because it usually reads as a promise rather than an explanation.

entries.name: in_medias_res
entries.description: An opening that begins mid-incident with no setup, leaving the viewer to catch up. Often paired with a later [flashback](#flashback) filling in how everyone got there; a [cold_open](#cold_open) only means the scene precedes the titles.

entries.name: intertitle
entries.description: A card of text cut between shots to carry dialogue, a date, a place or a comment. Tag the card itself; text burned over a live image is a caption, and the opening credits are a [title_sequence](#title_sequence).

entries.name: musical_number
entries.description: A self-contained song or dance sequence that carries a stretch of the story, staged and cut to the music. Tag the passage as a unit; a [montage_sequence](#montage_sequence) merely runs under music rather than being built on a performance.

entries.name: nonlinear_structure
entries.description: A piece whose scenes are not in the order the events happened, jumping about or running two timelines at once. Use it for the shape of the whole work; a single trip backwards is a [flashback](#flashback).

entries.name: picture_in_picture
entries.description: A small inset window sitting over a full-frame shot, showing a second view, a screen or a speaker. The main image still fills the frame, which is what separates it from [split_screen](#split_screen).

entries.name: post_credits_scene
entries.description: A short scene placed after or partway through the end credits, usually a joke or a hook for what comes next. Not to be confused with an [epilogue](#epilogue), which closes the story before the credits begin.

entries.name: prologue
entries.description: A self-contained opening passage set apart from the main story, often much earlier in time or told by a narrator. Unlike a [cold_open](#cold_open) it is not the first beat of the plot but a preface to it.

entries.name: recap_sequence
entries.description: Clips from earlier instalments assembled at the head of an episode to remind the viewer what happened. Built like a [montage_sequence](#montage_sequence) but made of reused material, and it sits outside the new story.

entries.name: set_piece
entries.description: A large self-contained sequence built as a showcase, planned around one location, stunt or effect and remembered on its own. Broader than [action_sequence](#action_sequence), since a musical number or a heist can be one too.

entries.name: training_montage
entries.description: A montage showing someone practising, building or getting fit, ending visibly better than it started. Distinguished from a plain [montage_sequence](#montage_sequence) by its arc: repeated effort with a measurable improvement at the end.

entries.name: film_within_a_film
entries.description: A passage showing a screen, a shoot or a projection inside the piece, so the viewer watches characters watching or making something. Distinct from [frame_story](#frame_story), where the inner material is simply told rather than screened.

entries.name: frame_story
entries.description: An outer scene, usually someone recounting events, that contains the main story and returns at the end. Tag the structure rather than the inner scenes; the return to the outer level is what makes it one.

entries.name: single_take_film
entries.description: A whole piece presented as one continuous shot from first frame to last, whether genuinely unbroken or stitched from hidden joins. Use for the film as a whole; a single scene done this way is a [oner](#oner).
